articles.title: Conversation Without Conversion: Evidence from Cross-Partisan Interactions on a Mobile Chat Platform
articles.abstract: Recent research on political persuasion suggests that narrative- and evidence-based messages can effectively change attitudes in settings such as canvassing, video presentations, and survey experiments. Yet less is known about how these persuasive strategies operate in two-way, cross-partisan political conversations. This study examines the relationship between persuasive message types, conversational reciprocity, and post-discussion attitudes using survey and text data from 966 U.S. participants engaged in anonymous one-on-one political discussions on DiscussIt, a mobile chat platform. I analyze how evidence-based arguments and personal narratives relate to both conversational interaction outcomes and measurable attitude change. Participants exposed to more personal narratives were more likely to perceive their conversation partner as influential and reported more positive conversational experiences, particularly when narrative exchanges were mutually reciprocated. In contrast, evidence-based exchanges were associated with lower perceived interpersonal influence, lower conversational enjoyment, and greater perceptions of relative knowledge. Despite these differences in conversational dynamics, neither persuasive strategy nor conversation structure was associated with significant changes in immediate or delayed political attitudes. Unlike studies of one-way persuasive messages, this research examines spontaneous peer-to-peer political conversations. Results suggest that persuasive strategies influence relational and experiential outcomes more than political attitudes.

articles.title: Body image and food content on TikTok: exploring the influence of TikTok videos on users’ body image
articles.abstract: The emergence of new media and its effects on users’ communication and behavior have been of interest to scholars. The study aims to add to the literature by analyzing the TikTok platform and the influence of TikTok's ‘What I eat in a day’ videos on body image. The research will draw on social comparison theory and utilize experiment as a method. The analysis extends the theoretical and methodological framework of videos about food on online platforms through the lens of TikTok.

articles.title: From content immunity to design accountability: youth social media addiction litigation after the Meta and YouTube negligence verdict
articles.abstract: This paper examines how recent youth social media addiction litigation, centered on the 2026 Meta and YouTube verdict, reframes harm as a problem of negligent design rather than third-party content. Using doctrinal legal analysis and policy synthesis, it argues that addictive-design and failure-to-warn claims may narrow Section 230’s practical reach, reshape understandings of duty and foreseeability, and support safety-by-design regulation. The paper positions youth litigation as a site for rethinking platform accountability in communication law.

articles.title: Implementing a State-Owned Utility's Promotional Discount Program: A Case Study of PLN's “Diskon Tambah Daya 50%” Initiative and Its Contribution to Customer Uptake and Business Sustainability
articles.abstract: This report presents a case study of the implementation of PT PLN (Persero) Unit Induk Distribusi Jawa Barat's “Diskon Tambah Daya 50%” (50% Additional Power Discount) program, a time-bound promotional initiative offering a 50% reduction in connection fees (Biaya Penyambungan, BP) to residential and business customers seeking to increase their electrical capacity. Conducted during the author's internship placement in the Commerce and Customer Management (Niaga dan Manajemen Pelanggan) division, this study documents the program's design, promotional execution, and operational realization, and situates the initiative within the broader context of customer-oriented marketing strategy and public-sector business sustainability practice. Data were gathered through direct participation, field observation, structured interviews with the internship supervisor, and review of internal program documentation. The author's principal contribution was the development of promotional media as part of the program's customer-acquisition strategy. As of 27 July 2026, program realization data show that 12,273 of a targeted 14,164 customers (86.65%) had completed payment, of whom 10,231 (83.36%) had been technically activated, generating Rp6.99 billion in connection-fee revenue and 14.63 MVA of additional contracted capacity. Six of the unit's service areas (Depok, Bandung, Cimahi, Bekasi, Sumedang, and Gunung Putri) exceeded their assigned targets. The findings illustrate how coordinated cross-unit implementation, multi- channel promotional communication, and time-bound pricing incentives can jointly support both short-term revenue objectives and longer-term customer base expansion for a state-owned utility. The report concludes with practical reflections on program execution and recommendations for strengthening future thematic promotional initiatives within PLN's customer management function. Keywords: promotional pricing, connection-fee discount, customer acquisition, state-owned enterprise, business sustainability, PT PLN (Persero)

articles.title: You Have My Attention: Offline Events and the Temporal Dynamics of Online Harassment in Politics
articles.abstract: The online harassment of politicians has become a defining feature of contemporary digital politics. While existing research has documented the forms and consequences of online harassment, less attention has been paid to how salient offline events shape its temporal dynamics. This study examines the relationship between salient offline events, such as wildfires and political resignations, and online harassment directed at Canadian federal Members of Parliament (MPs) on YouTube throughout 2024. We find that while a baseline level of harassment is consistently present, salient offline events are associated with short-term fluctuations in harassment, with comments increasing in the few days following an event. However, enduring structural factors, particularly MPs' gender and political party affiliation, are stronger predictors of harassment than offline events. By foregrounding time as an analytical dimension, this research advances our understanding of how offline events shape the temporal dynamics of online harassment while highlighting the structural factors that sustain it.

articles.title: Is the Justice Cascade Over? Accountability in an Era of Impunity
articles.authors: Averell Schmidt, Kathryn Sikkink, Geoff Dancy
articles.abstract: The emergence of individual criminal accountability for war crimes, mass atrocities, and the violation of human rights is among the most dramatic normative developments in international politics during the past half-century. Yet, recent political events -- from contestation of the International Criminal Court to the election of populist leaders opposed to legal accountability -- have fueled widespread concern that the world is returning to an era of impunity. In this article, we document a sharp global decline in human rights prosecutions since 2010 and develop a theory to explain this trend. We argue that human rights accountability requires a government willing and able to supply justice and a domestic audience that demands it. After 2010, the demand for prosecutions decreased in states with responsive governments and increased in states with the types of governments least likely to supply justice. We test this argument using an original dataset of all international, foreign, and domestic human rights prosecutions initiated between 1970 and 2023. Consistent with our theory, we show that the global shift is driven by a reduction of prosecutions in domestic courts and that together supply and demand factors are strongly predictive of domestic trial initiation. Our argument and findings indicate that the global decline in prosecutions is both a sign of success and a cause for concern. While past legacies of violence were addressed in openings created by democratic transitions, contemporary democratic backsliding risks denying justice to today’s victims.

articles.title: ANALYSIS OF BUDGET MANAGEMENT EFFECTIVENESS IN SUPPORTING PERFORMANCE ACHIEVEMENT OF THE ORGANIZATION FOR EARTH SCIENCES AND MARITIME (ORKM), NATIONAL RESEARCH AND INNOVATION AGENCY
articles.abstract: This report examines the effectiveness of budget management at the Organization for Earth Sciences and Maritime (ORKM), a research organization under Indonesia's National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN), during fiscal year 2025. The analysis is motivated by an apparent tension in ORKM's reported figures: a budget realization rate of approximately 87.4% (IDR 11.003 billion against a ceiling of IDR 12.59 billion) coexisted with full achievement of DIPA-funded output targets and a Budget Execution Performance Indicator (IKPA) score of 95.80, categorized "very good." Rather than treating this combination as self-evidently positive, the report interrogates it using document analysis of ORKM's internal planning and performance records (Terms of Reference, Work and Budget Plans, DIPA, and the 2025 Performance Report) together with participatory observation gathered during a practical work placement with ORKM's Program and Finance Team from June 29 to August 29, 2026. Effectiveness is assessed through Duncan's (1973) three-dimensional framework (goal attainment, integration, and adaptation) supplemented by a SWOT analysis to derive development strategies. The findings indicate that ORKM's budget management is effective in a qualified sense: output achievement and inter-document integration are strong, and the organization adapted successfully to shifts in grant disbursement schedules, yet component-level IKPA scores reveal a persistent planning weakness in the correspondence between the Cash Disbursement Plan (RPD) and actual realization, particularly for grant transactions. The report concludes that a single aggregate metric, whether the absorption rate or the IKPA score, is insufficient to characterize budget effectiveness, and recommends that ORKM prioritize strengthening RPD planning accuracy and digitalizing its verification workflow. As an internship-based report grounded in secondary documents and observation rather than primary data collection, the analysis is interpretive in nature and intended as a foundation for further empirical inquiry.

articles.title: The Role of Financial Literacy in Mediating the Influence of BSI Mitraguna on the Growth of MSMEs in Aceh
articles.authors: Yenny Irawan, Diana, Heri Fajri, Mariana, Zahriatul Aini, M Yazid AR
articles.abstract: This study investigates the influence of BSI Mitraguna financing on the development of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in Aceh, with particular attention to the role of financial literacy. Using a quantitative explanatory research design, the study focuses on active BSI Mitraguna financing recipients in Aceh. Respondents were selected based on specific criteria, including a minimum duration of financing engagement and ongoing MSME operations. Data were gathered through a structured questionnaire using a Likert scale and analyzed using the Structural Equation Modeling--Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS) method with SmartPLS software. The results reveal that BSI Mitraguna plays a significant role in fostering MSME growth. It not only provides financial capital but also contributes to improving the financial literacy of MSME actors. Furthermore, financial literacy serves as a crucial intermediary, enhancing the effectiveness of financing in driving business development. These findings suggest that microfinance programs are more impactful when integrated with financial education tailored to the specific needs of local entrepreneurs. Ultimately, this study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on Islamic microfinance by demonstrating that the synergy between financing and financial literacy is essential for sustainable MSME development. It also provides practical implications for policymakers and financial institutions to design integrated financing models that not only support capital access but also strengthen entrepreneurial capacity, thereby enhancing long-term economic resilience and inclusive growth

articles.title: Distributional Validity and Calibration of a Korean Synthetic Persona Panel for Digital and AI Service Use: A Secondary-Data Validation Against the Korea Media Panel Survey
articles.abstract: Synthetic personas based on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as substitutes for human survey respondents, yet systematic validation outside English-speaking contexts remains scarce. This secondary-data study evaluates how well a Korean synthetic persona panel (NVIDIA Nemotron-Personas-Korea), conditioned into Gemini 3.5 Flash (primary) and EXAONE (comparison), reproduces digital and AI service-use distributions from the KISDI Korea Media Panel Survey. Sex-and-age-stratified panels of about 8,000 personas per model answered the survey's own items - eight service-use indicators and eight innovativeness and acceptance constructs - and were compared against weighted survey estimates. The overall mean absolute error (MAE; RQ1) was 15-19 percentage points (pp), with binary item-mean correlations of 0.69-0.90. Segment error (RQ2) across five demographic axes was 15-19 pp, with between-group gaps up to 52.4/36.2 pp (Gemini/EXAONE). Errors followed model-specific signatures: an age stereotype with low anchoring (Gemini) versus an acquiescence-consistent level bias (EXAONE). Reference-year analysis was consistent with temporal misalignment driving most generative-AI overestimation, whereas short-form underestimation was framing-sensitive. Holdout calibration on 30% of the real data (RQ3) roughly halved sex-by-age cell MAE (18.9 to 8.6, 15.9 to 6.7 pp) - yet direct estimation from the same real subsample was far more accurate (3.6 pp), and the correction did not transfer across time. The calibrated panel retained an advantage only under extremely scarce real data (about 100 responses) and, for one model, for unobserved segments. Persona-narrative conditioning beat demographic-only conditioning, but neither surpassed simple real-data baselines. Synthetic panels are thus not survey substitutes; their value is diagnostic, with operational use confined to settings lacking real data.

articles.title: Coal Discharge Operations at a State-Owned Rail Logistics Terminal: A Case Study of Process Coordination and Information Flow at PT Kereta Api Indonesia's Tarahan Terminal
articles.abstract: State-owned rail logistics operators in emerging economies face a persistent tension between procedurally mature physical operations and underdeveloped digital coordination infrastructure. This case study examines the coal discharge process at PT Kereta Api Indonesia's (PT KAI) Tarahan Terminal in Lampung, Indonesia, drawing on 30 days of structured participant observation, document analysis, and informal interviews conducted during an internship in the Freight Transport (Angkutan Barang) unit. The discharge cycle—from rangkaian inspection at Tanjung Enim Baru, loading at the Train Loading System, transit to Tarahan, and unloading via the Rotary Car Dumperis mapped end-to-end and evaluated against operations management, supply chain management, and management information systems perspectives. While the physical workflow adheres closely to standard operating procedures and is supported by a structured document chain (Berita Acara Muat, Berita Acara Bongkar, Waktu Peredaran Kereta Api reporting), a SWOT analysis reveals that operational coordination remains dependent on informal, unstructured channels (principally WhatsApp) for transmitting time-sensitive information such as train circulation schedules and equipment-hindrance reports. This creates traceability gaps and latency risk that the formal procedural infrastructure does not, by itself, resolve. The study synthesizes these findings into a SWOT–TOWS strategy matrix and proposes a centralized digital monitoring dashboard alongside a direct-communication protocol (e.g., handheld radio) for time-critical disruptions at the Rotary Car Dumper interface. The case contributes a grounded, practice-level illustration of how digital-transformation and liquidity/resilience logics documented in prior public-sector operations literature (Indrajaya et al., 2026) manifest at the operational front line of a state logistics enterprise and offers actionable recommendations for terminal-level information governance.

articles.title: Standardizing Business Process Documentation for Operational Transition: A Case Study of Employee Administration Data Entry at PT Telekomunikasi Indonesia (Persero) Tbk

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Organizational transitions that transfer operational activities from internal units to external partners depend heavily on the availability of standardized process documentation. This study examines the business process of Employee Administration (EA) Kedinasan data entry within the Employee & Organization Data Operation (EODO) unit of PT Telekomunikasi Indonesia (Persero) Tbk, undertaken as part of the company's preparation to transfer data-entry activities to an external partner, PT Infomedia Nusantara. Using a descriptive-qualitative case study approach grounded in Business Process Management (BPM) theory, the study maps the existing (as-is) process through direct observation, documentation review, and discussion with field supervisors, and evaluates it using SWOT analysis to identify internal and external factors shaping the transition. The findings show that although the EA Kedinasan process already possesses a structured workflow supported by verification and approval checkpoints and a centralized SAP-based system, its documentation remains fragmented across multiple work instructions and lacks an integrated reference that can function effectively as a knowledge-transfer medium for an external partner. The study recommends the consolidation of Business Process diagrams, Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), Work Instructions, and a Playbook into a single coherent documentation package, which was implemented in part during the internship. Beyond its immediate organizational relevance, the case illustrates a broader tension in business process transitions: technically sound processes can still generate transition risk when explicit-knowledge artifacts are not consolidated for an external audience. The study contributes a practitioner-grounded account of how BPM and knowledge-transfer principles operate in a real outsourcing transition within a large Indonesian state-owned enterprise, and offers implications for organizations preparing similar administrative transfers.

articles.title: Media Accountability in the Age of Social Media in Nigeria
articles.authors: Adriel Ekozin, Omeiza Robinson Ofuje, Ekhareafo, O. Daniel, Daniel Ezegwu
articles.abstract: This study examined media accountability in the age of social media in Nigeria, focusing on the challenges and opportunities presented by digital communication technologies to ethical journalism and professional media practice. Using a library-based research approach, the study draws on books, journal articles, policy documents, media reports and relevant online scholarly materials to critically analyse the evolving accountability landscape within the Nigerian media environment. The study was anchored on Social Responsibility Theory and Accountability Systems Theory. Findings revealed that although Nigerian media institutions and regulatory bodies have made efforts to adapt to digital media through fact-checking initiatives, editorial reforms and policy regulations, significant gaps remain in ensuring ethical compliance, combating misinformation and rebuilding audience trust. The study concludes that strengthening media accountability requires greater commitment to professional ethics, responsible journalism, digital fact-checking, media literacy and robust institutional frameworks that protect freedom of expression while promoting responsible digital communication.

articles.title: HIERARCHICAL METHODOLOGY OF DMYTRO KRIVENKO: THE LIMITS OF DIALECTICS AND LEVELS OF PHYSICAL KNOWLEDGE
articles.abstract: This article reconstructs the philosophical and methodological programme of Dmytro T. Krivenko (1941–1994) as a level-sensitive approach to scientific and philosophical thought. Its historical basis comprises his publications of 1973–1988 on quantitative concepts, informational levels, rational inheritance, and the coarse-graining of complex systems; his 1991 formulation of a “hierarchical model of human cognition”; and manuscripts completed during his lifetime and published posthumously as Prynat i prynatyka (1996). The article argues that Krivenko did not merely add the notion of levels to a universal dialectical scheme. He distinguished the functions of general-philosophical, logical-methodological, and discipline-specific scientific levels. General philosophy could orient inquiry, but it could not replace measurement, mathematical constructions, models, limiting transitions, or empirical testing. Dialectics thereby ceased to operate as a self-sufficient algorithm of cognition and became one possible heuristic instrument within a broader hierarchical methodology. Five central elements of this programme are examined: the formation of physical quantities, informational levels, the growth of informativeness, rational inheritance, and coarse-graining. Scientific development is understood neither as the simple accumulation of facts nor as a universal movement through thesis, antithesis, and synthesis. A successor theory selectively preserves confirmed observations, relations, procedures, and limiting results while changing the ontology and structure of explanation. Coarse-graining shows how knowledge may advance through a controlled loss of detail. The anthropological and political dimension is reconstructed through the concepts of the Prynat and Prynatics. The Prynat is a holistic configuration of three levels of human Nature—the biological, the social or “sociumal,” and the spiritual—together with the individual forms through which they are expressed. All three levels are necessary, but the spiritual has the highest normative status because it integrates biological and social existence with freedom, dignity, and responsibility. Krivenko associates the absolutization of the biological with extreme nationalism and Nazism, the absolutization of the sociumal with communism, and the integrative spiritual level with democracy. Finally, Krivenko’s programme is compared with contemporary discussions of emergence, effective theories, multilevel ontology, and later applications to quark and exploratory preon models. These comparisons are not retrospective attributions, but tests of his central principle: a deeper description is scientifically meaningful only when it preserves validated knowledge, defines its domain of applicability, constructs explicit transitions between levels, yields independent consequences, and remains open to empirical falsification.

articles.title: Spatial mobility and the risk of dropping out of vocational education and training in Germany: Costs, resources, and returns
articles.abstract: Vocational education and training (VET) dropout disrupts school-to-work transitions. While spatial mobility is an important strategy for accessing VET, little is known about how it relates to subsequent dropout. Drawing on a cost-benefit perspective, this study examines whether first-year VET dropout differs by spatial mobility and whether these differences vary with resources available to bear mobility-related costs and returns that may offset them. We use representative longitudinal data from the German National Educational Panel Study linked to administrative geospatial data. Logistic regression models distinguish non-mobile students from those mobile within and between regional labor markets (RLMs) and assess heterogeneity by parental socioeconomic status (SES), VET wages, realized occupational aspirations, regional attractiveness, and regional person-environment match. Predicted dropout probabilities are approximately three percentage points higher for mobility within RLMs and four points higher for mobility between RLMs than for no mobility. These mobility-related differences decrease with increasing parental SES for both mobility types. Higher VET wages correspond to smaller dropout differences for mobility within RLMs, whereas greater realization of occupational aspirations corresponds to smaller differences for mobility between RLMs. Higher regional attractiveness shows a similar pattern only for mobility within RLMs, while higher regional person-environment match coincides with smaller dropout differences for both mobility types. Overall, mobility-related dropout differences vary with available resources and realized returns. The social patterning of mobility-related dropout differences may contribute to inequalities in school-to-work transitions, underscoring the importance of considering spatial mobility and regional contexts in research on youths’ educational decision-making.

articles.title: Toward Interethnic Peace
articles.abstract: General conditions conducive to interethnic peace are examined through the successful experiences of the post-slavery, multiethnic societies of Réunion and Mauritius. Intimacy, openness to others, and solidarity are identified as key characteristics of Creole societies that facilitate the emergence of attributes shared across individuals—a prerequisite for the construction of a harmonious society regardless of skin color. This congruence of values, conceptualized as surface hybridity and represented by the concept of the Creole envelope, was initially fostered by forced miscegenation. It subsequently deepened during the post-emancipation period through growing solidarity in response to recurring hardships, including natural disasters, deadly epidemics, and prolonged economic depression. Because most multiethnic Creole societies did not evolve into peaceful and cohesive communities, we highlight the importance of appropriate political institutions and, more specifically, the central role of human dignity as a foundational value. Drawing inspiration from natural systems and models of collective behavior in both animals and humans, we argue that dignity serves as the linchpin aligning uprooted Creole individuals with common political institutions, which serve as a societal template. Inspired by biomimetic assembly models, we suggest that surface hybridity may constitute a sufficient condition for the emergence of a peaceful and enduring multiethnic society by fostering the convergence of certain values across ethnic groups while preserving their distinctive core values.

articles.title: International development partnerships and nonprofit capacity in Ghana: an integrative review with practitioner evidence

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: International development partners route a substantial share of assistance through civil society, yet only a small proportion of this funding reaches organisations based in partner countries directly. This paper asks under what funding and partnership arrangements international support can strengthen Ghanaian nonprofits while preserving local ownership and organisational autonomy. I combine an integrative review of scholarly and policy literature with telephone consultations conducted in July 2026 with representatives of eleven Ghanaian nonprofit organisations using a common set of open-ended questions. The evidence indicates persistent funding volatility, restricted support for institutional costs, barriers to direct grant access, and significant administrative burdens. I argue that support is more likely to strengthen local organisations when it is predictable, reaches the institution as well as the project, uses proportionate access and reporting requirements, and preserves local authority over priorities. Practitioner accounts also locate part of organisational fragility in domestic regulatory and operating conditions that donor reform cannot address. International funding reform and improvements in Ghana's enabling environment therefore need to proceed together.

articles.title: Competency Restoration Timeliness in Washington Under Trueblood 2018-2026
articles.abstract: Objective. A federal court found Washington State's competency-restoration system unconstitutional in 2015 for making defendants found incompetent to stand trial wait months in jail for a psychiatric bed; the State did not appeal that part of the injunction, and the Ninth Circuit left it undisturbed in 2016. The system did not turn around until after years of escalating enforcement culminating in a contempt finding and a $100 million fine. We ask whether that timing reflects sustained federal-court enforcement, and what drove it. Methods. We built an open monthly panel of Washington's Trueblood court-monitor data (January 2018–May 2026; 1,033 rows) and analyzed statewide inpatient restoration timeliness as an interrupted time series against a 7-day admission standard, alongside a jail-based-evaluation comparator on a looser clock. Results. The system was non-compliant for six years (annual median waits 28.0–63.5 days; compliance rarely above 30%, and 6% in March 2023 when the median wait peaked at 97 days), then improved sharply — median 5.0 days, 90.4% average compliance, holding over 26 months of continued oversight. The gain concentrated in bed-dependent services: both moved sharply while the bed-independent comparator's median wait moved +0.0 days on the raw split and a small but statistically significant −1.3 days on the regression estimator; coding by Washington's Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) attributes an average 90.8% of restoration delays to bed availability, though almost all of that coding predates the turnaround. All facilities improved; demand rose, not fell (Limitations). Conclusions. The improvement coincided with sustained Trueblood enforcement; this single-jurisdiction design supports association, not causation. The open, re-executable panel offers an independent compliance monitor complementary to the state's own.

articles.title: Good jobs, bad jobs, and the upward mobility potential of self-employment
articles.abstract: Most of the self-employed eventually return to paid employment. Prior research documents a penalty for former entrepreneurs re-entering paid employment but assumes a background of a standard job. Could entrepreneurship facilitate upward mobility for workers from casual employment backgrounds instead? For these workers, entrepreneurship can demonstrate previously hidden ability through observable business performance and provide them with a more stable base from which to seek standard employment. I investigate the earnings and employment trajectories of former entrepreneurs in India. Among those who previously worked in non-salaried employment, those with a short spell in self-employment experience a small penalty. Those with a longer, successful spell reap large earnings premiums and transition to salaried employment at higher rates than matched controls. In contrast, most former entrepreneurs from salaried backgrounds face persistent earnings penalties. These results reveal how the upward mobility potential of entrepreneurship depends on alternative employment options. By relaxing assumptions of stable employment backgrounds, this study extends the careers lens to the modal entrepreneur globally.

articles.title: Sense of place based on shared imaginaries for caring for the chinampa socio‑ecosystem
articles.authors: Ana Paula Margain Leon, Lakshmi Charli Joseph, Jesús Mario Siqueiros-Garcia
articles.abstract: Sense of place refers to the meaningful connection that people establish with a space, which can either motivate or inhibit environmental care. Understanding the mechanisms that strengthen this connection is central to promoting sustainable ways of cohabiting a place. This study proposes imagining desired futures as a mechanism to mobilise a sense of place among young people from Xochimilco in Mexico City and to catalyse new forms of care. Drawing on a qualitative methodology, the study shows that this connection became a conscious, deliberate act that enabled reflection and collective visibility of bonds with place. The findings suggest that imagining futures expands the possibilities for collective care.

articles.title: The Institutional Production of Causation: Predictive Classification and the Limits of Self-Attested Transparency in AI Governance
articles.abstract: Predictive classifications do not merely describe the world. Once embedded in institutional decisions, they alter access, scrutiny, opportunity and the evidence from which their own validity is later assessed. This Perspective extends that account of institutional causation to the governance of AI systems. Providers and oversight bodies classify incidents as authorised or unauthorised, material or immaterial, in scope or out of scope, and verified or unverified. These labels allocate investigative attention and determine which records are preserved, which populations are examined and which explanations remain available. When the institution issuing a classification also controls the evidence capable of testing it, a closed evidentiary loop can result: the initial category defines the inquiry, the inquiry defines the evidence population, and that population ratifies the category. Detailed disclosure may then remain self-attested rather than independently verifiable. The discovery disputes in The New York Times Company v. Microsoft Corporation et al. illustrate the institutional difference between disclosure and contestability. Court-ordered preservation, negotiated sampling, de-identification and controlled access did not decide the merits of the litigation, but they created an external forum in which evidence scope and negative assurances could be challenged. Transparent AI governance therefore requires more than publication. It requires institutional separation between the authority to classify and the authority to determine what evidence may test the classification.

articles.title: Making Sense of Machines: Ritualized Care, Agency Attribution, and Failure Interpretation in Human-Automation Encounters in India
articles.abstract: Machines in India are cared for, spoken to, honored, and blamed, well beyond ordinary use. New vehicles are blessed before their first drive, workshop tools are garlanded and rested during Vishwakarma Puja, and small tilak marks or deity images sit on machine casings without a second thought. Human-computer and human-robot interaction research has rarely asked what these everyday practices do to the way people read a machine that hesitates, fails, or behaves unexpectedly. This paper reports a formative, mixed-method study of how adults in India make sense of ambiguous automated behavior, and whether caring for and personifying machines shapes how they read that behavior. A survey of 156 adults gives a baseline for how common these practices are, how people explain failure, how much agency they grant a machine, and what they want from a system when it fails. Machine-care practices turned out to be almost universal: 96% of respondents reported at least one. In a scenario where a vehicle fails before an important journey and then starts again on its own, 62% chose a relational or meaningful explanation alongside the technical option they were also given, and 60% expected a machine they had looked after to perform well in return. The interviews complicate that last figure: most of what looks like relational trust there is closer to an ordinary belief that upkeep improves performance. The orientation toward the recovering vehicle did not carry over evenly to newer technology, either. About a third of respondents said they trusted AI more than mechanical machines and expected it to “know better,” a view far more common among younger respondents. I read the survey alongside twenty-one semi-structured interviews, conducted in Hindi and English with photographs and short scenarios and analyzed thematically. Across both urban and rural lives, people mostly treated machine care as ordinary maintenance, not as a belief that machines are conscious. That relational orientation showed up again and again, but it also ran into real limits: in platform work, in closed or inaccessible design, and among people who reject it on rational or minority-faith grounds. There is no single Indian view of machines here. Region, generation, religion, and class produce real differences, and I treat those differences as central to the findings, not as noise to explain away. The paper offers three things: a documented instrument set for studying culturally situated automation sensemaking, along with an honest account of where its measures blur together and how they could be sharpened; a preliminary vocabulary connecting ritualized care, agency attribution, and failure interpretation; and an early design agenda for settings where machines carry meaning beyond what they do.

articles.title: Beyond Prediction Error: A Decision-Theoretic Model of Resistance to Belief Updating
articles.abstract: Agents often decline to adopt revisions their own inference supports. We propose that posterior computation and belief implementation are distinct operations: Bayesian inference produces candidate revisions, and a cost-sensitive decision — an endorsement gate — determines whether a revision becomes the operative belief, P(U = 1) = σ(β₀ + β_E·E − β_C·C), with E the posterior displacement (Bayesian surprise) and C the expected reorganization cost of implementation. The model adds a gating layer between inference and representational change without modifying inference. We derive the logistic implementation probability conditional on a specified random-utility representation, give a dynamic formulation with partial updating, and evaluate parameter recovery, estimator behavior, and rival discrimination across a reproducible simulation programme spanning identifiability, estimator pathology and correction, rival discrimination, adversarial severity, and design calibration, with four formal analyses. The theory’s confirmatory content is one preregistered discriminative program with two logically ordered stages, formalized as fixed-sequence gatekeeping. Stage one — state-trace coupling under selective single-channel cost manipulation — separates the gate from independent channelwise commitment thresholds: a reversed, two-dimensional association is fatal. Stage two — content-specificity in a matched-displacement, within-class two-belief design — separates a content-bearing operative state from content-general or content-conditioned threshold policies: a certified null belief-by-cost interaction is fatal, as is content-specific staleness without an implicit–downstream gap, or a positive pattern that retrieval probes expose as trace competition. An identity-conditioned threshold policy is shown to be observationally and psychofunctionally equivalent to the gate under a representationalist construal — underdetermination of ontology, not the victory of one vocabulary — so the empirical content rides on the shared structure. A severity-gated verdict table fixes in advance which outcomes are fatal, which supportive, and which merely silent. Every claim is flagged confirmatory or interpretive; alternatives are organized by a working taxonomy — empirical rivals, equivalent redescriptions, artifact families — whose placements are functional for the program, not verdicts on any account’s standing as a theory. The program opens with a pre-Stage-1 validation pilot whose success criteria are measurement properties, never effects, gated by preregistered traffic-light progression criteria. The register is held fixed throughout: a successful future experiment could support, at best, a shared, channel-coupled, content-specific, use-level operative constraint on belief use; the endorsement gate is the most parsimonious interpretation of that structure, and the choice of interpretive vocabulary is downstream of the result, not part of it.

articles.title: The development of subsistence effort and skill among BaYaka foragers
articles.authors: Sheina Lew-Levy, Erik Ringen, Lucie Benoit, Yann R. Ouamba, Adam Boyette, Sarah Pope-Caldwell, Lee Gettler, Alyssa N. Crittenden
articles.abstract: Why humans have such long childhoods is an evolutionary puzzle. Childhood may represent a developmental period for the acquisition of cognitive and physical skills needed to exploit the complex hunted and gathered resources typical of our species’ subsistence niche. Childhood may also be an extended period for cooperating with kin, and by extension, reaping inclusive fitness benefits. Studies in contemporary hunter-gatherer communities show that subsistence proficiency peaks in adulthood. Yet, there is considerable inter-individual variation in food returns, with some children efficiently collecting specific resources from a young age, and others exceeding their daily caloric needs. To understand why some children are more productive than others, here we investigate the association between subsistence effort and skill development among Congo Basin BaYaka foragers. BaYaka rely on hunting, gathering, fishing, and small-scale horticulture for subsistence. We measured subsistence effort and food production over a six-week period in a forest camp with 52 residents aged 0 to 70 years. We analyzed these data using a Bayesian latent hierarchical model. We found that 50% of subsistence skill was achieved by age 15. Both subsistence skill and effort peaked in adulthood. Further, we found a negative age-adjusted correlation between effort and skill, suggesting that lower-skilled individuals participated in subsistence more frequently. Overall, our findings show that children can meaningfully reduce day-to-day dependence on adults, which over evolutionary time, may have helped offset the cost of extended human childhood.

articles.title: Determinants of Patent Applications across European Regions: Evidence from Panel Estimators, K-Means Clustering and Predictive Validation
articles.authors: Angelo Maurizio Galiano, Giuseppe Dell'Erba, Alberto Costantiello, Angelo Leogrande
articles.abstract: Europe measures the innovative performance of its regions largely by counting patents, and allocates public resources accordingly. This paper asks what regional patenting actually reflects, drawing on Regional Innovation Scoreboard data for 245 European regions observed annually between 2016 and 2023. Three candidate drivers are considered: the research effort of firms, the intensity of formal collaboration between the research base and industry, and the propensity to protect intangible assets through trademarks. Business research effort emerges as the dominant correlate throughout, science–industry collaboration as a weaker but consistent one, and trademark activity as a positive one, suggesting that firms which protect brands are not forgoing patents but exercising a single appropriation capability across several instruments. Two findings carry implications beyond measurement. Regional innovative capacity proves remarkably immobile: differences between regions account for roughly 95 per cent of the variation in the data, and differences within a region over the eight years for the remainder, so the short-run movements on which policy evaluation typically relies carry very little information, and the returns to innovation investment should be sought over horizons far longer than a programming cycle. And when the 245 regions are grouped into four innovation profiles rather than treated as a single population, the relationship that holds on average holds almost nowhere in particular: it is strong among leading and lagging regions, statistically absent in the largest group, and displaced by brand-led appropriation in a fourth group of 27 regions whose innovation is real but largely non-technological. Uniform innovation policy prescriptions and uniform managerial benchmarks are correspondingly difficult to justify.

articles.title: Beyond the Rural Designation: Geographic Aggregation as a Justice Problem in Psychiatric–Mental Health Nursing

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Objective: To argue that the geographic category "rural," as operationalized in disparities research and federal shortage-area designation, conceals the rural populations who fare worst, and what follows for psychiatric–mental health (PMH) nursing. Methods: Critical analysis of literature on rural mental health disparities, rurality measurement, and racially and sexually minoritized rural populations, spanning 2002, when the field was urged past counting rural disorder toward how place shapes it, through 2026. Results: Prevalence findings have stayed inconsistent for two decades, substantially because rurality is measured dichotomously. On disaggregation, the rural–urban axis often proves the wrong one: among American Indian and Alaska Native veterans, urban–rural comparison yields no significant difference while comparison with White veterans yields large ones. Because shortage-area designation is geographic, the aggregate does not merely describe disparity; it drives allocation. Conclusions: Aggregation is not a neutral convenience. A category that renders the worst-off invisible and governs resource distribution is a justice concern for a specialty supplying much of rural America's mental health workforce. PMH nursing should assess structural position rather than residence, adopt continuous and intersectional measures of rurality, and contest designation methodology as professional advocacy.

articles.title: Love at First Swipe: Online Dating and Relationship Outcomes in Europe
articles.abstract: This article examines whether unions formed through online dating differ from other unions in relationship trajectories across nine European countries. Using harmonised Generations and Gender Survey data, I estimate country-specific survival and current-union models for union dissolution, marriage, shared biological childbearing, relationship satisfaction, and break-up consideration. Adjusted dissolution hazards are higher in Austria, Estonia, and Croatia, lower in Germany, and not significant elsewhere or among recent unions. Among surviving unions, online dating is more often associated with lower marriage and shared childbearing, especially in Croatia and the United Kingdom, than with poorer relationship quality. Overall, online dating appears more strongly associated with how unions are institutionalised and converted into family life and the findings do not support the idea of a uniform pan-European relationship difference associated with online dating.

articles.title: Governments as Adopters and Regulators of AI: A Challenge for Democracy?

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This paper explores the dual role of governments as both adopters and regulators of artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on the implications for democratic governance. As AI technologies become increasingly embedded in public administration – from policymaking to service delivery – they offer opportunities for improving efficiency and personalization but also raise concerns about transparency, accountability, and fairness. To deal with these questions, this paper examines how AI is framed as a policy problem, the regulatory approaches adopted in different political systems, and the politicization of AI governance. It also analyzes the democratic risks posed by algorithmic decision-making, polarization, and corporate concentration of power, while highlighting the potential of AI to enhance democratic quality through improved public services, inclusive discourse, and citizen engagement. The paper concludes by identifying key areas for future research, including legitimacy, trust, regulatory design, and equity in AI governance.

articles.title: Optimizing Recovery Value in Public Asset Disposal: Business Process Mapping (As-Is vs. To-Be) Analysis of State-Owned Asset Sales and Write-Offs at Indonesia's Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Efficient management of state-owned assets (Barang Milik Negara, BMN) is a critical determinant of fiscal accountability and non-tax state revenue (Penerimaan Negara Bukan Pajak, PNBP) optimization in public sector organizations. This study examines the process of proposing, verifying, and executing the sale and write-off of low-value BMN (below IDR 100 million) at the Bureau of Finance and State Assets, Secretariat General, Indonesia's Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs (KOMDIGI), where delegated approval authority under Minister of Finance Regulation (PMK) No. 4/PMK.06/2015 was, in practice, insufficiently leveraged to accelerate administrative throughput. Employing a qualitative, participant-observation-based case study design conducted over a six-week practicum period, this research applies Business Process Mapping (As-Is vs. To-Be) to document the existing workflow, identify bottlenecks and non-value-added activities, and design a redesigned process architecture. The As-Is analysis reveals three structural inefficiencies: (1) duplicated manual verification between spreadsheet-based checklists and the State Asset Management Information System (SIMAN); (2) recurrent data mismatches across unit nomenclature, asset codes, and book values; and (3) an undifferentiated verification pathway that fails to exploit the risk-based delegation of authority for low-value assets. A SWOT matrix further situates these findings within the organization's internal capabilities and external opportunities, generating SO, WO, ST, and WT strategic alternatives. The proposed To-Be process (anchored on system integration, a risk-based fast-track lane, and standardized correspondence templates) is theorized to compress processing lead time and thereby preserve the economic value of assets pending disposal, directly reinforcing recovery value and PNBP contributions. This study contributes to the limited empirical literature on business process reengineering in Indonesian public asset governance and offers a replicable diagnostic-to-design framework for other line ministries operating under similarly delegated regulatory regimes.

articles.title: Measuring and Repairing Document Conversion Errors in the Michigan Child Welfare Policy Manual
articles.abstract: Author Note (August 18, 2026): This preprint is currently undergoing systematic review and revision. An updated version will be posted upon completion. Readers are encouraged to consult the latest version of the manuscript. Child welfare practice is governed by documents written for people to read. A state policy manual specifies how quickly a caseworker must see a child after the child returns home, and it does so in a PDF laid out for the eye. Any system that answers questions from such a manual must first convert it into text, and that conversion step is rarely measured. This study measures it. Five test documents were constructed to replicate the layout of the Michigan Children’s Protective Services Manual, with identifiers replacing its words. The identifiers run consecutively, so that a loss reads as a gap in a counted run and a person can see it without tooling, and each one ends in a check code, so that a converter driven by a language model cannot supply a convincing replacement for whatever it dropped. The same artifact is therefore verifiable by a person reading it and by a script counting it, and the tool under test cannot repair the evidence before either of them looks at it. Four converters were evaluated on the test documents, and the two generations of the commercial service were evaluated on the manual itself, for a total of 31 documents and 328 pages. No converter was adequate for every property required by a retrieval corpus. The older generation invented 43 section headings that appear nowhere in the source, and the corpus assembled from it labels a column in a contact-standards table with the wrong requirement, so it lists three contacts with each child at intensive risk, where the manual states one. The current generation’s cheapest tier deletes the opening line of every paragraph beginning Exception:, which is how this manual marks the cases a rule does not cover. None of these failures garbles the text. Each produces fluent prose that reads as policy and states a rule the manual does not contain. The study then reports a repair procedure that derives document structure from the PDF’s geometry, and fifteen checks that halt conversion if any fail. Every check passes across all 31 documents, measured against the same documents from which the repair rules were derived. A fourth failure property emerged only after presence, level, and order had all reached their best values: 380 paragraph boundaries across 200 of the 328 pages were marked in the source by vertical spacing that the converter does not read.

articles.title: Financial Risk Management Practices in a State-Owned Energy Enterprise: A Process-Based Case Study of Market Research Operations at PT Pertamina (Persero)

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Financial risk management (FRM) has become a strategic function within state-owned energy enterprises exposed to volatile commodity prices, exchange rate fluctuations, and interest rate movements. While a substantial body of literature examines the determinants and firm-level consequences of financial risk exposure and hedging behavior, comparatively little empirical or practice-based work documents how such risk-monitoring functions are operationally structured and executed within large state-owned enterprises (SOEs) in emerging markets. This study addresses that gap through a process-based case study of the Market Research sub-function within the Financial Risk & Insurance Center (FRIC) of PT Pertamina (Persero), Indonesia's national energy company. Using Business Process Modeling (BPM) with BPMN notation and a SWOT analysis supported by Internal Factor Analysis Summary (IFAS) and External Factor Analysis Summary (EFAS) matrices, this study maps the daily workflow of market monitoring and Morning Market Flash Report preparation, identifies operational strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats, and formulates strategic recommendations. The findings indicate that the process exhibits strong internal verification controls (a multi-tier review chain and the use of integrated tools such as Bloomberg Terminal and the FRAME application) but remains constrained by manual data-entry processes and tight pre-market deadlines. Positioned in Quadrant I (Growth/SO) of the SWOT matrix, the function is well placed to pursue an aggressive strategy centered on automation and standardization. The study contributes a practice-grounded account of financial risk monitoring operations that complements the predominantly econometric literature on FRM determinants and offers actionable recommendations for both corporate practice and academic curricula in financial risk education.

articles.title: From Search Engines to Answer Engines: Testing the Effects of Traditional and AI Search Engines on Belief in Misinformation
articles.authors: Kylan Rutherford, Zeve Sanderson, Jonathan Nagler, Joshua A. Tucker
articles.abstract: Counter to the advice in many digital literacy guides, recent research has demonstrated that using a search engine to learn more about false or misleading articles can actually incorrectly increase belief in the veracity of that news (Aslett et al. 2024). As the future of search turns to AI-powered search and chatbots, will AI be able to ameliorate this problem? To investigate this question, we recruited over 4,000 participants to assess the veracity of recent news articles, and evaluate how using either a traditional search engine (TSE) or an AI search engine (AISE) affects their assessments. We find that using the AISE (Perplexity) increases belief in misinformation at almost the same rate as the TSE (Google). We also find that search strategies which perform poorly on TSEs (e.g., copying and pasting links) may actually improve the utility of AISEs. We find no difference in the rate of unreliable links served.

articles.title: Political Talk in Nonpolitical Digital Spaces
articles.abstract: In recent years, scholars in communication and media studies have increasingly turned their attention to political discourse that emerges incidentally within ostensibly nonpolitical digital contexts. These political discussions not only permeate diverse online platforms and communities, but also carry significant democratic potential. Despite growing interest in the phenomenon, existing research remains fragmented across distinct theoretical traditions and lacks a coherent conceptual understanding. This article addresses that gap by reviewing studies in three epistemological orientations—post-positivist, interpretive, and critical—that can guide the analysis of political talk in nonpolitical digital environments. In doing so, it highlights how this group of phenomena can be understood and interpreted with different theoretical assumptions, thereby enabling scholars to better assess their communicative and political significance. This review offers a foundation for more integrative and theoretically informed research on the various dimensions of political expression in digital networked publics.

articles.title: Determinants of Wealth Inequality in the Game of Diplomacy: An economic and computational perspective
articles.authors: Julia Wlodarczyk, Andrew Zadrozny, Kripa Rajshekhar, Wlodek Zadrozny
articles.abstract: This paper presents the first comprehensive analysis of wealth inequality within the strategic game of Diplomacy, addressing a significant gap in existing literature, which typically focuses on tactics, cooperation, and deception rather than distributional outcomes. Utilizing an anonymized dataset of over 1 million records corresponding to players’ winnings (supply centers and all territories) at the end of the game, we calculate Gini coefficients to quantify inequality. The analysis reveals that Diplomacy exhibits moderate-to-high inequality (Gini = 0.56 for supply centers and 0.52 for all territories), comparable to real-world economies such as Spain or South Korea. Fractional logit and beta regressions reveal that wealth inequality in strategic environments is not merely a result of individual skills but is structurally shaped by institutional rules, communication, and path-dependent accumulation. In particular, higher player count and longer game duration are associated with increased inequality. Moreover, the possibility to engage in private communication significantly in- creases wealth disparities compared to no-communication environments, as it facilitates complex coali- tions and betrayals. However, high levels of overall communication activity tend to reduce inequality, though inequality in communication itself (dominance by one speaker) correlates positively with wealth inequality at the end of the game. Finally, preliminary results suggest the presence of AI agents has a significant impact on wealth distribution, confirming that Diplomacy is a relevant laboratory for studying human-AI collaboration and competition

articles.title: Local-Oriented Online Communities in Urban Communication Infrastructures: News Media, Engagement, and Emotion in 128 North American City Communities
articles.abstract: Local-oriented online communities (LOOCs) have become ubiquitous spaces for discussing national and local news as well as urban civic life, yet existing scholarship lacks a consistent framework to explain what shapes their behavioral and emotional outcomes across diverse contexts. This study applies Communication Infrastructure Theory (CIT) to conceptualize LOOCs as meso-level storytellers whose outcomes are shaped by their connections to broader storytelling networks. Analyzing 1,613,650 posts and 32,706,953 comments from 128 North American city subreddits over the full year of 2024, we examine how connections to mainstream media, local media, urban governance topics, and everyday urban life topics predict thread-level engagement and emotional expression. Results show that both mainstream and local media connections substantially increase engagement but correlate with more negative emotional expression. Urban governance topics increase behavioral engagement but elicit negative sentiment, whereas everyday urban life topics exhibit the inverse pattern, showing an engagement–negativity tradeoff.

articles.title: The Dynamics of LGBTQ+ Visibility and Demographic Shifts in the Philippines: A Sociological and Public Health Analysis
articles.abstract: The contemporary demographic landscape of the Philippines has witnessed a significant increase in the visible population of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer (LGBTQ+) individuals. Often colloquially and inaccurately characterized as an "overgrowth," this phenomenon represents a complex sociodemographic shift driven by heightened self-identification, evolving sociolinguistic frameworks, and progressive, albeit localized, policy environments. This comprehensive research report examines the multifaceted dimensions of LGBTQ+ population dynamics in the Philippines. Drawing upon national demographic surveys, sociological ethnographies, public health registries, and legal jurisprudence, the analysis deconstructs the mechanisms behind the increased visibility of sexual and gender minorities. The report investigates the profound public health challenges accompanying this demographic shift, specifically the escalating HIV/AIDS epidemic and pervasive mental health crises driven by minority stress. Furthermore, it explores the legislative stagnation of national anti-discrimination protections, the compensatory rise of local government ordinances, and the cultural integration of queer identity through linguistic innovations such as Swardspeak. Ultimately, the evidence suggests that the expanding LGBTQ+ population in the Philippines is not a sudden biological anomaly, but rather a sociological reclamation of space within a society navigating the tension between deeply entrenched post-colonial Abrahamic conservatism and pre-colonial traditions of gender fluidity.

articles.title: If it bleeds, it leads? Evaluating whether LLMs can identify what is newsworthy
articles.abstract: Journalists have always had to make the challenging decision about which stories to focus on and which stories to ignore. This paper investigates whether AI can assist journalists in identifying newsworthy stories from large databases. We first build a dataset of Canadian lobbying registrations, each labeled as "newsworthy" or "not newsworthy" based on whether a journalist covered it in a published article or not. We then systematically evaluate several AI models' ability to identify the one newsworthy registration within a batch of ten. The best models identify a single newsworthy registration with 22% accuracy, rising to 48% when allowed to select three, and to 52% when provided previous headline examples. Our results suggest that a filtering approach silently discards real stories, whereas allowing the model to rank registrations by newsworthiness ensures no information is lost. We conclude that while AI holds real potential to help identify leads, this is not possible without further investment in evaluation infrastructure, and even then, there is an important role for journalists to identify what AI misses, as it cannot replace their editorial judgment entirely.

articles.title: Counting the Accountability Gap: A National Freedom of Information Census of Public Clock Maintenance in England

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Who is responsible for a stopped public clock? This paper reports a national attempt to answer that question empirically, and argues that the pattern of non-answers is itself the finding. Two datasets were assembled. The first is a documented set of 402 stopped public clocks in Britain, collected by field observation and public contribution since 2007 and classified by current custodian; it is a floor, not a census. The second is a census of what English principal councils themselves know: Freedom of Information requests to all 314 principal local authorities, yielding 310 responses of which 187 were substantive, disclosing 566 council-managed clocks of which 70 (12.4%) were stopped. Of the documented set, only 26.4% stand on council-owned buildings, the one category where the Freedom of Information Act compels an answer about maintenance; roughly 74% stand on private, commercial, ecclesiastical or trust-owned buildings, beyond the reach of any public enquiry mechanism. I call this the accountability gap, and I present it strictly as a claim about reach, not cause: for three-quarters of documented failures, a citizen cannot even discover whose job the maintenance was. Direct approaches to some sixty private owners, met overwhelmingly with silence, corroborate the gap from the other side. The stopped public clock is proposed as a countable, photographable proxy for the dissolution of collective maintenance arrangements in the public realm, and the method as a replicable template for measuring accountability reach over any distributed class of shared assets.

articles.title: Agricultural technology and diversification to mitigate climate change-related issues in Chinese rice production: A farmers’ perspective
articles.authors: Qianqian Liu, Estelle Raveloaritiana, Xiaohan Huang, Xueqing He, ZengRong Zhu, Lei Wang, Thomas Cherico Wanger
articles.abstract: Agricultural technology (agri-technology) and diversification (agri-diversification) can advance sustainable agriculture and food security amid climate change, and combining them may amplify benefits. Yet farmers' knowledge and adoption remain poorly understood, limiting scalability. Here, we interviewed 1,352 rice farmers across three Chinese provinces spanning a climatic gradient. Farmers perceived climate change-related challenges mainly as production issues, with 82% reporting rising pest occurrence and 42% reporting health issues. Four of five agri-technology categories were both well known and widely adopted (>91% and >61%, respectively). By contrast, only three of seven agri-diversification categories were widely known (>64%), with most practices below 25% awareness. County-level factors—temperature, per capita gross domestic product and farmland fragmentation—were associated with awareness and adoption for many agri-diversification practices but few agri-technologies. Agri-diversification therefore remains under-recognized and underused, and depends more on local conditions than agri-technology. Targeted policy should promote the co-benefits of implementing both strategies together.

articles.title: Broad Fiscal Burden in Asian Energy-Transition Contexts: How Development Levels Condition Growth
articles.abstract: Asian economies face the challenge of reducing emissions while sustaining economic growth, yet the growth implications of environmental taxation remain uncertain. This study examines whether broad tax burden and energy-system conditions are associated with economic growth in Asia, whether the tax-growth relationship varies by development level, and whether renewable-energy context is more closely related to growth or environmental performance. Using an unbalanced country-year panel of 20 Asian economies from 1972 to 2024, the analysis applies fixed-effects regressions with country and year effects and country-clustered standard errors. Because direct energy-tax measures are unavailable, tax revenue as a share of gross domestic product (GDP) is used as a broad fiscal proxy. The baseline model shows no statistically significant relationship between tax revenue and real gross domestic product per capita growth, while the estimated coefficient is small and negative. Income-group models suggest heterogeneity around this weak average association: the tax-growth relationship is negative for lower-middle-income economies but positive for upper-middle-income and high-income economies. Renewable-energy share does not significantly moderate the tax-growth relationship, but it is strongly associated with lower carbon intensity of output. These findings indicate that taxation’s growth associations depend on development level and not uniform across Asia, while environmental performance is more clearly linked to energy-system structure than to tax revenue alone. Policy should therefore avoid stand- alone tax instruments, pair fiscal reform with revenue recycling and household protection, and expand renewable-energy infrastructure.

articles.title: Cumulative Advantage in Job Quality: Career Trajectories and Inequality in Sweden, 1968–2022
articles.abstract: Cumulative (dis)advantage is well documented for wages and occupational prestige, but whether similar patterns characterize non-monetary working conditions remains unclear. This study examines career trajectories in job quality—job complexity, physical demands, negative stress, and flexibility—using Swedish Level-of-Living Survey panel data from 1968 to 2022 (5,042 respondents; 14,857 observations). We ask whether inequalities in job quality widen or narrow across career stages, whether social groups differ in within-career change, and whether workers who begin from more favorable positions subsequently gain more or less. We estimate adjusted inequalities across career stages using random-slope growth curve models and differences in within-career change using individual fixed-effects models. Job quality generally improved over the first 20–25 career years among cohorts born from the 1940s onward. Educational inequality was large and persistent: workers with more education held better jobs throughout and gained more within their careers. Gender inequality emerged over time: men and women began near parity, but men gained more. Within social groups, however, workers who started with better job quality improved less, indicating convergence. Adjusting for occupation reduced career-stage inequalities more than differences in within-career change. Thus, inequalities may widen between social groups even as differences within groups narrow over the career.

articles.title: Reversal of the Educational Gender Gap and Assortative Mating: Increasing Educational Hypogamy amid Persistent Age Sorting in Latin America
articles.abstract: Previous research has revealed a positive association between female educational advantage and the prevalence of educational hypogamy. However, age assortative mating, as a relevant feature in the process of union formation, has been overlooked. This study analyzes the effect of the decrease of the educational gender gap on the likelihood of being married and age and educational assortative mating among Latin American women. Data come from the harmonized microdata samples from the census rounds of eight Latin American countries from 1970 to 2010, available in the Integrated Public Use of Microdata Series International database. Binomial and multinomial logistic regressions were used to evaluate the effects of changes in the educational gender gap on the odds of being single and being assortatively mated in terms of age and education. Results suggest that changes of the educational gender gap had a negative effect on the probabilities of being married and they were associated with higher levels of educational hypogamy, whereas the patterns of age sorting were more rigid than the patterns of educational sorting.

articles.title: Comparing Information Disorder Policy: The Global Disinformation Policy Database, 2000–2023

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Comparative research on information disorder policy faces a dependent-variable problem: policies sharing a label differ in what they regulate, and policies regulating the same conduct carry different labels. The Global Disinformation Policy Database (GDPD) addresses this problem, coding 364 policies from 132 countries, 2000–2023, and decomposing each into label, information quality, regulated behavior, and intent standard. The decomposition shows that 57.7% of “disinformation” policies specify no intent standard, that policy growth predates the literature’s 2016 watershed, and that instruments have diversified away from criminal sanction along regional lines. The GDPD enables researchers to compare how governments conceptualize contested information.

articles.title: Increases in national origin disparities in ICE Arrests, 2025-26
articles.authors: Caitlin C Patler, Claire Morton, Avi Feller
articles.abstract: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has rapidly expanded operations since the January 2025 US presidential inauguration, raising concerns about profiling based on national origin or ethnicity. We assess this issue using administrative records on nearly 500,000 ICE arrests from November 2023 to March 2026, comparing per-capita arrest rates for unauthorized residents from Europe, Canada, and Oceania (EUCA) with those from all other regions (non-EUCA) in 2025-2026, relative to 2023-2024. We document two patterns that are inconsistent with claims of neutral enforcement. First, non-EUCA per-capita arrest rates rose substantially more than EUCA rates in the 14 months following the inauguration, both nationally as well as in every state and ICE jurisdiction with sufficient data. We estimate 217,000 excess non-EUCA arrests relative to a baseline scenario in which non-EUCA and EUCA arrest rates rose equally. Second, the largest disparities occurred among individuals without convictions apprehended in the community rather than via transfers from criminal custody, contrary to claims of targeting people with criminal records. Together, our findings document pervasive national origin differences in ICE enforcement at a time of acute legal and policy contention, raising new questions about the causes and consequences of these broad disparities.

articles.title: Delisting without co-migration: author communities before and after removal from Scopus
articles.abstract: Purpose: Delisting removes a journal from an index but not its authors. This study asks whether cohorts disperse or share destinations and whether concentrated inflow is associated with receiving journals’ subsequent delisting. Design/methodology/approach: The analysis reconstructs interval-valued delisting dates from successive Scopus lists, assigns delisted-journal event clocks to matched cohorts, and compares destination overlap with margin-preserving, opportunity-structured, and matched-observed benchmarks. A six-month-landmark discrete-time hazard model handles right censoring and administrative coverage-change exits. Findings: Across 136 stacks, delisted-journal output averaged 66.7% below the post-event reference path. For 121 cohorts, median observed-to-expected overlap was 2.40 under the opportunity-structured benchmark. Across 55 matched sets, delisted cohorts overlapped 10.6 percentage points less that references (95% CI [-0.14, -0.07]), a difference that predated delisting. The highest inflow quartile had 4.66 times the adjusted hazard of the lowest (95% CI [2.04, 10.64]), based on 78 events and 99.3% censoring. Research limitations: Delisting is non-random, so estimates are descriptive contrasts, benchmark deviations, and conditional in-sample associations. Practical implications: Synthetic benchmarks establish residual cohort structure; matched observed cohorts test whether it distinguishes the event-defined population. Originality/value: The study provides a two-stage design for event-specific concentration claims. Pairing a constrained randomisation with matched observed cohorts reversed the substantive conclusion

articles.title: European and US companies communicate less about diversity post-Trump election
articles.authors: Loureiro Lopes, A.I. (Ana Isabel), João Gonçalves

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: We analyzed the social media posts of top 20 European and US companies for their Diversity related content before (2024) and after (2025) the election of Donald Trump. We find that there was a decline in diversity related content in 2025 both in the US and in Europe, with the biggest drop being registered in the US. From all social media content, 6,7% of posts by US based companies in 2024 included diversity related topics, while in 2025 only 1,3% were about diversity. For European companies, the scenario is similar. In 2024, 12,6% of social media posts by European companies touch upon diversity content which dropped to 7,0% in the same period of 2025. In general, European companies posted more on diversity than American companies both in 2024 and in 2025. These results show us that while the drop in diversity related talk by corporations was more accentuated in the US, other geographies seem to also replicate the trend.

articles.title: Integrating Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) in Participatory Research Practice with Young Children with Disabilities. A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract: Objective: Young children with disabilities often face barriers to participation in research, as many of them do not use verbal speech. This limits the representation of their views concerning designing research processes, policies, support systems or education. Assuming that the integration of Alternative and Augmentative Communication (AAC) into research methods could be a suitable approach to deconstruct these barriers, this review explores the implementation of AAC into participatory research with this group. Method: A scoping review was conducted (Tricco et al., 2018). Following a systematic search in scientific databases and two screening rounds, 8 studies were included. Full texts were analysed concerning the use of AAC and the modalities of children’s communication by means of Qualitative Content Analysis (Kuckartz & Rädiker, 2024). Results: Only three studies reported unaided or low-tech AAC-use for data collection. Additionally, a wide range of other child-friendly modalities for children to express themselves were identified which facilitated communication, but did not classify as AAC. These strategies were mostly applied during data collection (e.g. within interviews), while decision-making concerning the research process (e.g. choosing a research question of methods) relied on verbal communication. Conclusion: The potential of AAC for participatory research has not yet been realized to its maximum.
