Nevertheless, other multimodal and child-friendly forms of facilitating children’s communication also are very valuable. Both forms should be extended to support children’s decision-making concerning the research process. Future research should focus on using this potential to involve all children – including those with disabilities - into participatory research.

articles.title: The Geography of Life Chances and Intergenerational Mobility
articles.abstract: We have entered a new era of soaring inequalities in income and wealth, patterns driven by a highly differentiated landscape of opportunity. This economic reality has propelled the geographies of intergenerational mobility and life chances to the forefront of the social science agenda. While geographers are increasingly engaging with these topics, the field of economic geography provides a critical, yet underutilized, theoretical foundation for this work. This chapter proposes the People-Experience-Places (PEP) framework, a model for analyzing the geographic differentiation of life chances across space and time. Drawing from core schools of thought within economic geography, the framework identifies the foundational mechanisms that produce spatially differentiated opportunity regimes and their impact on intergenerational mobility. The chapter concludes with a call for economic geographers to return to the core concerns of understanding and addressing inequalities in livelihood possibilities.

articles.title: A good climate for solutions? The adaptation of solutions journalism within Surinamese climate journalism
articles.abstract: This study explores how climate journalists’ role conceptions and media system constraints shape their perceptions and practices of solutions journalism. It does so through a reflexive thematic analysis of in-depth interviews with five of the six practicing climate journalists in Suriname. Findings suggest that journalists express concerns about environmental injustices, particularly those affecting Indigenous communities, yet remain reluctant to adopt interventionist roles. They define their primary task as informing and providing context rather than promoting specific solutions, with objectivity functioning as a professional norm and strategic resource in a fragile media environment where access to sources is precarious. Solutions journalism is further reinterpreted in the Surinamese context, with solutions only introduced after problems have been thoroughly portrayed. Overall, the findings suggest that professional role conceptualizations and solutions journalism approaches cannot be generalised along Global North/Global South lines but are instead reshaped within specific political, economic, and structural conditions.

articles.title: Through Rose-Tinted Smart Glasses: Tech Myths and the Normalisation of Wearable Harms
articles.authors: Milica Stilinovic, Joanne E. Gray, Sanika Vekhande, Ben Egliston, Wenqi Tan, Ryan Stanton, Marcus Carter
articles.abstract: Smart glasses are marketed as lifestyle devices that enhance productivity, creativity, and social connection. However, a growing body of evidence suggests these devices are facilitating new harms relating to privacy, bystander consent, and human agency. This paper examines how branded social media content contributes to the normalisation of smart glasses usage while obscuring their associated risks. Focusing on Instagram as a key promotional environment, this study conducts a quantitative content analysis of 768 branded posts featuring Meta’s market leading Ray-Ban glasses alongside emerging competitors Xiaomi, Rokid, Even Realities, and XReal. We analyse how smart-glasses practices are visually and narratively represented and evaluate how recording visibility is addressed and how potential harms are downplayed or obscured. Results suggest that even within highly commercial advertising environments, social and ethical harms remain embedded in the representation of the technology itself. Branded content therefore plays a critical role in legitimising these devices through the construction of powerful technological myths.

articles.title: Linking Media Effects with Political Talk: A Theoretical Review
articles.abstract: Political talk has been a central focus of political communication research. However, grounded in a micro-conversational perspective often fall short in explaining the emergence of diverse forms of political discourse, as well as recent declines in both news use and participation in political talk. By presenting a macro-structural view of political talk and revisiting two classical media effects, this article provides a theoretical review on how agenda-setting and framing effects of general media and mediated communication can shape political talk, across cognitive, affective, and behavioral dimensions. Theoretically linking media effects with political talk contributes to explaining macro-structural conditions for various political talk to happen, integrates both traditional and non-institutionalized forms of political talk, and generates a set of propositions and research questions to guide future empirical inquiry.

articles.title: Japanese has effectively only two accent patterns: A quantitative and information-theoretic approach to lexical predictability
articles.abstract: Japanese pitch accent is traditionally described as a free accent system allowing up to n + 1 possible patterns for an n-mora word. However, Japanese accentuation is heavily constrained by factors such as word length, prosodic structure, and lexical stratum, leading to the hypothesis that the system fundamentally reduces to only two dominant patterns: unaccented and thematic (antepenultimate). Evaluating this claim requires moving beyond raw counts of empirically attested patterns to quantify the skewness of their distribution. In this study, we introduce information-theoretic metrics, specifically Shannon's conditional entropy and ecological effective numbers of diversity, to measure the uncertainty an diversity of accent patterns in a representative sample of 8,173 Japanese common nouns. Our findings show that while overall pattern richness reaches the theoretical maximum (7 patterns), global effective diversity remains low (3.12 by type frequency, 3.43 by token frequency). Crucially, with knowledge of word length, prosodic structure, and lexical stratum the number of accent patterns is reduced to effectively two (2.1) dominant patterns, providing a precise, quantitative validation of the two-pattern hypothesis. We further demonstrate that prosodic structure is the single most informative factor, reducing accentuation uncertainty by 23%, and that native nouns exhibit greater residual uncertainty than Sino-Japanese and foreign words. Finally, the strong alignment between type and token results confirms that dictionary-based word lists closely mirror natural speech distributions in phonological diversity.

articles.title: Analysis of the effectiveness of the procurement and receipt process of goods in supporting retail store operations
articles.abstract: CV Chiko Mitra Abadi is a retail company in Bandung Regency operating a one-stop shop concept that combines a supermarket, furniture, and playground facilities. Because the company depends on suppliers for all merchandise sold, the effectiveness of its procurement and receipt of goods process is central to maintaining stock availability, data accuracy, and smooth store operations. This report was compiled from Practical Work carried out in the administrative section of CV Chiko Mitra Abadi from June 29 to August 7, 2026, during which the author was directly involved in supplier data management, Purchase Order (PO) preparation, goods receiving, SKU/PLU verification, price and margin updates, and the preparation of promotional media. The report describes the company's procurement and receipt workflow, identifies the operational obstacles encountered during implementation, and evaluates the process using SWOT analysis. The findings show that CV Chiko Mitra Abadi already applies clear procedures supported by formal Purchase Order documentation and generally good coordination among the Administrative, Receiving, warehouse, and supplier-facing functions. However, several weaknesses remain, including administrative tasks that are still performed manually, price and margin updates that are not yet system-integrated, and inspection procedures that slow down when incoming volumes are high, compounded by suppliers' delivery reliability. Based on these findings, the report recommends greater use of integrated information systems, closer and more structured supplier coordination, standardized receiving checklists, and regular employee training, together with a more consumer-centric view of how these administrative improvements ultimately affect customer experience on the sales floor. These recommendations are intended to help the company run its procurement and receiving process more effectively and sustain the smooth operation of its retail store.

articles.title: Agentic AI in Data Commons and GLAM: What Role for the Model Context Protocol?
articles.abstract: The emergence of the agentic web, in which AI agents autonomously navigate online services to accomplish complex tasks, poses urgent questions for digital commons and GLAM institutions (Galleries, Libraries, Archives, and Museums). This paper reports on a crosssectoral workshop held at the Bibliothèque nationale de France, which examined the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as a new infrastructure layer for regulating agentic access to open knowledge resources. Drawing on presentations by practitioners and researchers across the library, archive, museum, performing arts, open knowledge, and open science sectors, the paper documents emerging MCP experiments, identifies transversal governance challenges, and synthesizes the outcomes of a collective prospective scenario-building exercise. Key findings include: the reframing of MCP server deployment as an editorial act with significant implications for data representation and institutional authority; the identification of critical capacity gaps between API-ready and non-API-ready organizations; and the recognition of MCP governance as a site of broader advocacy for the commons and public goods within the agentic web.

articles.title: Long-term population resilience: an archaeological perspective
articles.abstract: This paper critically examines whether archaeological and palaeoenvironmental research on past population resilience has focused on analytically unsuitable questions and scales. It argues that the nature of the material record constrains the identification of resilient adaptations in the commonsense use of the term, particularly when studies privilege short-lived “pulse” disturbances such as catastrophic events. Instead, the paper advocates greater attention to long-term processes that better align with the temporal granularity of archaeological data. It further interrogates dominant theoretical frameworks derived from complex adaptive systems, highlighting their limited empirical operability, and contrasts them with ecological definitions of resilience grounded in measurable dynamics. The discussion introduces the distinction between resilience and robustness, suggesting that past socio-ecological systems may have favored heterogeneity and non-optimisation to mitigate risk, obviating the need for ‘resilience’ throughout the vast majority of human history. Ultimately, the paper is a call for recalibrating expectations, methods, and narratives to better capture long-term adaptive variability in human history.

articles.title: The Post-Neolithic Anomaly? How ‘Civilisation’ Might Be An Aberration in Human History.
articles.abstract: For the majority of its existence, our species did not live in settlements, did not have agriculture, writing or metallurgy. These are all features of the Holocene Epoch, and the global human population during most of the time since the start of that epoch remained both low and relatively constant until the beginning of the 19th Century, accelerating through the 20th Century, following the Industrial and Agrarian Revolutions. The enormous population, and the complex, planet-wide capitalist technological civilisation on which they depend, but which also exploits them, are now faced with numerous dangers, which are likely to prove insuperable.

articles.title: Unraveling why, how and under which conditions do green interventions improve health and wellbeing in deprived neighborhoods: a realist review
articles.authors: Jonáh Stunt, Jessica C. Kiefte-de Jong, Birthe Jongeneel-Grimen
articles.abstract: Background: Approximately 75% of the European Union population lives in urban areas, a proportion expected to exceed 80% by 2050. Urban green spaces (UGS) are widely recognized for promoting health and well-being. Interventions that increase or improve UGS have been associated with greater use of green spaces and higher levels of physical activity, contributing to positive physical and mental health outcomes. Such interventions may be especially beneficial for lower socioeconomic status (SES) groups living in deprived neighborhoods. However, systematic reviews report inconsistent and sometimes contradictory evidence regarding the positive health effects of UGS interventions in these areas. Without understanding the essential elements and processes underlying effectiveness, it remains unclear why certain interventions succeed and how they can be transferred to other contexts. To address this gap, a realist review was conducted to identify and map the mechanisms and processes through which UGS interventions may improve health in deprived neighborhoods. Methods: An iterative realist review methodology was used to uncover why, how, for whom, and under what conditions UGS interventions are effective. Initial theory development drew on input from residents and professionals, as well as scientific and grey literature. The review followed the RAMESES Quality Standards for Realist Reviews. Retrieved studies were systematically screened and iteratively analyzed to develop Context–Mechanism–Outcome Configurations (CMOCs) and an overarching Realist Programme Theory. Results: Sixteen articles were synthesized, resulting in 17 CMOCs grouped into five themes: social capital, lower thresholds for physical activity, enjoyment of nature, safety, and community involvement. These themes clarify how and under which circumstances UGS interventions can positively influence health in deprived neighborhoods. Key mechanisms include social processes (e.g., increased social support and cohesion), physical processes (e.g., greater physical activity and reduced stress and fatigue), and psychological processes (e.g., mental restoration and improved concentration). Community participation emerged as a cross-cutting mechanism that can activate all pathways by bringing residents together across demographic differences. Environmental, individual, social, and cultural factors shape the extent to which these mechanisms are triggered. Conclusion: UGS interventions operate through multiple, interrelated dynamics. Effective implementation requires attention to diverse (environmental) improvements and to the local mechanisms at play. Tailoring interventions to community needs is essential to ensure that residents of deprived neighborhoods fully benefit from urban green spaces.

articles.title: Municipal Political Representation and Housing Affordability
articles.abstract: Housing affordability has become a pressing issue in many communities, and municipal governments play a critical role in shaping the character and quantity of local housing supply. At present, however, we know little about the extent to which municipal politicians are equipped to represent their constituents’ preferences on housing supply and housing affordability. In this paper, we combine a nationally representative survey of Canadians with a survey of more than 700 mayors and councillors in municipalities across Canada to explore (a) the extent to which politicians align with their constituents in their housing policy attitudes and (b) the extent to which politicians' views are more representative of more privileged local residents, such as homeowners. Across nine concrete housing policy proposals, we find strong evidence of macro-level policy representation: when local communities are more supportive of a housing policy proposals, local politicians tend to be more supportive as well. We also find that politicians' attitudes on housing are not more aligned with privileged local residents; instead, elite-mass alignment is primarily shaped by ideological congruence. These findings suggest that slow progress on housing policy is driven not by policy misalignment between politicians and citizens, but instead by patterns of local mobilization and "neighborhood defender" behavior.

articles.title: Migration as Labor Governance: Empire, Replaceability, and Worker Power
articles.abstract: Why does substantial worker mobilization generate effective leverage in some settings but not in others? This article argues that the answer depends partly on labor governance: the institutions through which labor is recruited, legally differentiated, disciplined, and rendered replaceable. Extending the Empire Theory of Migration (ETM), I distinguish the imperial production of migrant labor from its subsequent organization as labor supply. I develop the argument through three historically connected farmworker campaigns: the National Farm Labor Union’s struggle against the DiGiorgio Fruit Corporation, the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee, and the United Farm Workers. Their divergent outcomes—failed recognition, incomplete institutionalization, and contingent bargaining success—show that mobilization generates leverage only when workers and their allies can raise the costs of employer resistance despite employers’ access to alternative labor supplies. Drawing on Ernesto Galarza’s political economy of the Bracero Program, undocumented recruitment, deportation, and labor contracting, the article identifies recruitment, regulation, and legitimation as interconnected dimensions of labor governance. Empire produces migrant labor; labor governance organizes that labor as labor supply; replaceability conditions worker power.

articles.title: A History of Macroeconomics
articles.authors: Francesco Sergi, Beatrice Cherrier, Aurélien Saïdi, Pedro Duarte, Aurélien Goutsmedt, Matthieu Renault, Juan Acosta
articles.abstract: This book offers a history of macroeconomics (the study of “the economy” as a whole) from its inception in the interwar period to today. Its novelty is twofold: it goes beyond a history of theories to cover a wider range of macroeconomists’ practices; it relies on a growing body of historical research, challenging misconceptions commonly disseminated in macroeconomics textbooks. This is not “yet another history of macroeconomics”. It is one that should strike scholars and students in macroeconomics as novel. Such a history is needed because macroeconomics textbooks project a particular “identity” of the field, derived from a specific historical narrative, in which the field evolved through theoretical “revolutions” and “battles” between “schools of thought” initiated by “great men”. We argue that this misrepresents the actual dynamics of macroeconomics. Our history conveys a different perspective, highlighting a more diverse set of characteristics (what macroeconomics is about) and practices (what macroeconomists do). We emphasise how macroeconomics has always relied on the combination of research agendas (theoretical, mathematical, empirical, and computational); how the interaction with other fields (notably microeconomics and econometrics) has been constant; and how the field has been shaped by a cast of researchers with diverse geographical and institutional origins (some working within academia, others in policymaking institutions and private organisations). We bring these many dimensions together through a simple chronology outlining four periods: birth (1920s-1940s), bridges (1950s-1960s), frictions (1970s-1980s), and constellations (1990s-2000s).

articles.title: Moving targets? Life-course dynamics in intergenerational mobility
articles.authors: Roujman Shahbazian, Erik Bihagen, Edvin Syk
articles.abstract: Research on intergenerational mobility assumes that individuals reach occupational maturity, typically around age 35, allowing occupational positions to be treated as stable destinations and mobility to be summarized by a single estimate. We argue that this assumption is difficult to reconcile with contemporary occupational careers. If occupational positions continue to evolve throughout adulthood, intergenerational mobility may itself be a life-course process rather than a fixed parameter. Using retrospective occupational histories from 27 European countries and the United States, we first show that occupational mobility commonly extends well beyond the age conventionally assumed to mark occupational maturity. We then analyze Swedish population register data, estimating parent–offspring associations across every combination of parental and offspring ages between 27 and 56. Rather than converging to a stable value, intergenerational associations vary systematically over the life course, peaking in mid-adulthood before declining. These findings challenge the view that age-related variation primarily reflects measurement error. Instead, they suggest that intergenerational mobility is continuously reshaped by intragenerational mobility over the life course, raising the more fundamental question of whether there exists a single intergenerational mobility parameter to recover.

articles.title: The Stratification Engine: A Recurrent Mechanism of Compound Exclusion

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Resource deprivation cuts two ways. It blocks access to new technologies, and scarcity can narrow the cognitive bandwidth needed to use them. I formalise this as the Resource–Technology–Cognitive (RTC) chain, in which disadvantage compounds at the interfaces between layers, so that exclusion multiplies rather than adds. Cognitive inheritance, reconstituted each generation through early-life conditions rather than genetically transmitted, is posited to carry this compound disadvantage across generations unless those conditions change. I trace the chain across eight technological transitions as an illustrative basis, and derive three falsifiable propositions about sequential causation, super-additive amplification, and intergenerational moderation. The AI transition restructures access and skill demands simultaneously, and the next cohort's starting conditions are already forming.

articles.title: Public Attitudes Toward National Border Controls
articles.abstract: How do citizens evaluate national border controls? In this paper, we argue that while public attitudes toward national border controls are not necessarily fixed, they are primarily interpreted through the lens of migration. To test this argument, we conduct an original survey in Germany and combine open-ended questions with a conjoint and an information experiment. The findings show that migration is not only strongly associated with national border controls, but that the reduction of irregular immigration is also the most important dimension when evaluating these controls. Nonetheless, the findings provide evidence that attitudes toward these controls are not fully fixed: Information on the benefits of the Schengen free travel agreement modestly increases support for border-free travel and reduces support for national border controls. The results have important implications for how the public assesses national border controls in the European context.

articles.title: Exploring the impact of inference method, character coding scheme, and cognacy criterion on phylolinguistic inference: The case of the Japonic language family
articles.authors: Thomas Pellard, Kenan Celik, Reiko Aso, Yosuke Igarashi, Masatoshi Matsunami
articles.abstract: The application of phylogenetic methods to linguistic data requires several critical methodological choices, yet their relative influence on the resulting trees remains poorly understood. This study conducts a systematic sensitivity analysis to evaluate the impact of three key factors: (1) the phylogenetic inference method (neighbor-joining, maximum parsimony, and Bayesian inference), (2) the character coding scheme (binary vs. multistate), and (3) the cognacy (i.e. homology) criterion (root-based vs. stem-based cognacy). Using the Japonic language family as a model, we generated a diverse set of phylogenetic trees and compared them using multiple tree metrics and distance measures between trees. Variance partitioning through distance-based redundancy analysis reveals a clear hierarchy of influence: the choice of inference method is the primary driver of variation between trees, followed by the character coding scheme, while the cognacy criterion exerts a comparatively minor effect. Specifically, we show that the choice of inference method fundamentally shapes tree topology, whereas the character coding scheme impacts branch lengths and evolutionary tempo. While maintaining a consistent and transparent definition of cognacy remains good practice, our results indicate that the choice of one definition over another does not always lead to a significant loss of phylogenetic signal. Therefore, phylolinguistic research should prioritize first and foremost the rigorous selection of inference method.

articles.title: When statistics outlive their geography: asynchronous propagation of a secondary medical area redefinition across Japan's national health data infrastructure — a measurable instance of institutional debt

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Health-system geographies are periodically redefined, but the national statistical products that encode them are updated on independent schedules. We report a natural experiment in how such a redefinition propagates. Effective 1 April 2024, Akita Prefecture consolidated its secondary medical areas (SMAs) from eight to three — the only SMA reorganization under Japan’s 8th Medical Plan cycle — reducing the national SMA count from 335 to 330. We examined how three national data products required for SMA-level analysis of the same reference year (2024) encoded the change, by comparing their SMA code sets and validating municipal re-aggregations against published totals. The Physician, Dentist and Pharmacist Statistics 2024 (census date 31 December 2024; released December 2025) and the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare’s municipality–SMA correspondence table (version dated April 2026) encode the new three-SMA definition. The 11th NDB Open Data, released June 2026, tabulates fiscal-year 2024 claims — all generated after the redefinition took effect — in the superseded eight-SMA geography. No product declares the vintage of its zone definition as metadata; the divergence surfaces only as unexplained code mismatches — and, for three zone codes reused across definitions, as silent mis-joins — observable from published artifacts alone. We interpret this as a measurable instance of institutional debt — the divergence between legally effective definitions and those encoded in infrastructure, with reconciliation labor externalized to analysts — quantifiable along three axes (lag, affected population, repairability). Contrasting England’s centrally remapped response to its 2022 commissioning-geography transition, we propose that zone-level statistics be published as versioned views over stable unit identifiers with mandatory definition-vintage metadata.

articles.title: Geodemographic Inequalities in Battery Electric Vehicle Adoption across UK Neighbourhoods
articles.authors: Alex Singleton, Ian Philips, Jillian Anable

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Battery electric vehicle (BEV) adoption is an important contributor to the decarbonisation of road transport in the UK and other OECD countries, yet uptake remains highly uneven between places. This paper examines the geography of privately kept battery electric vehicles across UK small areas using quarterly DVLA vehicle licensing records, linked geodemographically to the 2021/22 UK Output Area Classification. The analysis measures observed private vehicle ownership at neighbourhood scale, enabling within local authority variation to be examined directly. The results show that BEV penetration is strongly right-skewed, with adoption concentrated in affluent professional neighbourhoods, prosperous suburban and rural areas, and dense urban cores with relatively small but rapidly electrifying private fleets. Lower uptake is associated with neighbourhoods characterised by rented tenure, terraced housing and flats, where access to private off-street charging is likely to be more constrained. Partitioning the national time series by geodemographic type reveals that the aggregate adoption curve is composed of distinct trajectories, with some early-adopting neighbourhood types showing signs of slower recent growth while later-adopting groups continue to accelerate. Residuals from the geodemographic baseline are spatially clustered, indicating that neighbourhood composition alone does not explain the geography of adoption. The paper demonstrates the value of combining administrative vehicle records with geodemographic classification to identify where BEV adoption is leading, lagging and diverging from demographic expectation, with implications for a more equitable rollout of charging infrastructure and transport decarbonisation policy.

articles.title: Cultures of Civil Crisis Preparedness

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Recent crises, including pandemics, extreme weather events, and humanitarian crises, have demonstrated informal civil society’s role as a crucial first responder to crisis situations. Yet crisis management research and policy have largely treated informal civil society as a spontaneous resource activated only during response and recovery and lack a conceptual understanding of informal civil society in the crisis preparation phase. This article develops a theoretical framework for understanding cultures of civil crisis preparedness: shared repertoires of perceived responsibilities and preparedness strategies through which civil society anticipates and prepares for future crises. The framework specifies how a community's crisis perceptions shape both responsibilities and strategies, how trust networks enable mutual coordination, and how institutional crisis management approaches, geographical exposure, and authorities' crisis communication shape informal civil society's role in preparedness. It thereby enables analysis of how people come to imagine their own and others' responsibilities before crises occur, and why cultures of civil crisis preparedness vary across national and local contexts.

articles.title: Prospective Travel Diary in Tourist Decision-Making

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This research note introduces a new image-based tool that integrates inspiration and co-creation in tourist decision-making. Grounded in prospective memory – a concept developed in psychology literature- the tool enables participants to mentally simulate and visualize a future trip, constructing a fictitious travel diary through illustrated cards. This approach serves as both a research method for studying decision-making processes and a practical tool for tourism professionals. We explore its theoretical foundations, applications, and potential to enhance tourist engagement and travel booking experiences.

articles.title: Deliberative, affective, and experiential risk in crisis response: Fears of responders and people in crisis
articles.authors: Andrew David Eaton, Megan Wheeler Rowe, Claire Ryder, Amanda Mathew, Sandra Kwan, Jenny Hui, Brandon Barksdale, Leyna Lowe
articles.abstract: Mental health crisis response is diverse and evolving, with ongoing debate about outcomes for people in crisis, the appropriateness of different responses, and the role of police. Crisis encounters combine three forms of risk assessment: reasoned judgments (deliberative), emotional responses (affective), and gut feelings (experiential). This qualitative knowledge-to-action study consisted of interviews with 33 Canadian and American key informants in crisis response (e.g., responders and people with lived experience of crisis encounters). Interpretive phenomenological analysis was employed by a large and diverse coding team on data pertaining to shifting dynamics and experiences of risk. Findings address: a) the governing logic of risk in crisis response, as risks are triaged and translated yet remain subjective and uncertain; b) constant perceptions of risk in crisis encounters that shift based on the scene and mental health discourses; and c) a double-bind to police involvement, where responders fear risks to themselves and others on scene and seek security and stability in police but people in crisis fear police involvement. Risk moves from deliberative to experiential via affective emotions on the scene. This study identified sustained reliance on police by responders, even within civilian-led, non-police alternative crisis response teams. Police remain a form of first response, co-response, and backup or escalation support, heightening risk for people in crisis, despite focused efforts to de-task police from crisis calls.

articles.title: Backcasting Semantic Risk Indicators in Historical Travel Advisories: Enriching a Longitudinal Web Corpus
articles.abstract: Travel warnings can affect the political and economic situation in the target countries. However, data to systematically investigate these links are lacking. Previous work has introduced and validated a crawler pipeline to obtain time series of government-issued travel advisories via the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine. Governments may change the type and amount of information they provide in their advisories. For example, the United States began to provide numerical travel warning levels for individual countries and tags to categorize advisories in 2018. We illustrate an approach to using these \textit{labeled} data points to extend the variable for travel advisories before 2018 and for other issuing countries. In addition, we show how to extract additional information, such as whether the advisory concerns an entire country or specific regions or cities. This paper documents a further step towards a harmonized and unified dataset and a multilingual text corpus of government-issued travel advisories for the social sciences, humanities, and beyond.

articles.title: Population Development In The Roman Empire
articles.abstract: This paper addresses the problem of reconstructing the population development of the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire despite the scarcity, inconsistency, and indirect nature of the available evidence. Its primary objective is to produce a continuous population curve spanning from 508 BC to AD 395, which is internally consistent in the assumptions of underlying growth and other factors over time. To achieve this, the study critically integrates multiple methodological approaches, including Beloch’s area-and-density estimates, Lo Cascio’s revisions, and Scheidel’s demographic critiques, alongside archaeological, economic, and comparative demographic evidence. By combining these methods and cross-validating their results, a coherent framework is established for estimating both population levels and growth rates. It adopts moderate empire-wide growth assumptions, 2-3‰ annually, while allowing for significant variation between core and newly incorporated territories. This enables the interpolation between key chronological benchmarks and the extension of estimates across periods lacking direct evidence. The resulting reconstruction yields a continuous demographic trajectory showing the full consequences of the growth assumptions.

articles.title: Ready for What? Rethinking AI and Robotics Preparedness for Adoption and Policy

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Efforts to accelerate AI and robotics adoption require evidence about where communities are prepared to act and where support is still needed. However, conclusions based mainly on average differences between people or stakeholder groups can obscure relationships that emerge when the same person evaluates different challenges. We address this problem using a repeated card-based survey in which 982 participants provided 15,200 evaluations of 17 AI and robotics challenges. Each challenge was rated on common 1-5 measures of significance, complexity and readiness, where readiness refers to perceived community preparedness and available resources rather than personal competence or realised adoption. Because each participant evaluated multiple challenges, the design separates stable differences between respondents from challenge-specific deviations within the same respondent. This distinction materially changes the interpretation of preparedness. Within the same respondent, a challenge rated one point more complex than their usual level is associated with approximately 0.21 points lower readiness ($p<0.001$). By contrast, respondents who generally rate challenges as more complex do not systematically report lower readiness ($p=0.29$). Significance is positively associated with readiness, while unusually high complexity modestly weakens this challenge-specific alignment. These relationships also vary strongly across challenge families, and professional background remains associated with adjusted preparedness assessments. On applied cards, confidence, trust and related perceptions provide substantial additional information about readiness, including for held-out participants. For policymakers and organisations, the findings show that averaging across stakeholders can hide challenge-specific barriers. Readiness assessments should therefore preserve both differences between stakeholder groups and variation within the same stakeholders across challenges. Effective adoption and literacy strategies should ask not only \emph{who} appears ready, but \emph{which challenges} they find unusually difficult and whether the likely constraint concerns implementation, capability, assurance or resources.

articles.title: Technological complexity and the nature of adaptive problem-solving in small-scale societies
articles.authors: Marcus J. Hamilton, Briggs Buchanan, Robert S. Walker, Mark Collard, Nicholas Gala
articles.abstract: Technological complexity is a defining eature of human adaptation, yet the processes determining how much technology societies require remain poorly understood. Existing explanations emphasize environmental risk, resource productivity, or demographic factors, but provide limited insight into why technological systems respond differently across subsistence economies. Here, we propose that technological complexity reflects the computational burden imposed by environmental uncertainty. In seasonal environments, survival requires solving a sequential decision problem in which risks accumulate multiplicatively across the year, increasing demand for technological buffering. Technologies reduce this uncertainty but are costly to produce and maintain, generating an optimization problem balancing risk reduction against technological costs. We further argue that niche construction fundamentally alters this relationship by smoothing environmental variability and transforming exogenous uncertainty into managed, endogenous processes. From this framework we derive the prediction that technological complexity should increase with environmental seasonality among hunter-gatherers but become increasingly independent of climate as niche construction intensifies. We test these predictions using data on toolkit richness and component-part diversity from 127 small-scale societies. We find the richness of hunter-gatherer technologies increases exponentially with environmental seasonality, whereas farming technologies remain largely invariant across climatic regimes. These findings suggest that technological complexity responds to the informational and computational demands environmental conditions impose. More broadly, these results imply that agriculture represents not simply a new mode of energy acquisition, but a transition in the computational architecture of human adaptation, in which farming reduces the effective depth of adaptive problems by restructuring the environments that generate uncertainty.

In the last decade, some teams received significant investment such as the Paris Saint German in France, with a significant investment from some Arab Companies.

articles.title: 从宗教圣地到茶道名片——汉口亚历山大·涅夫斯基教堂的百年变迁 From Sacred Sanctuary to Tea Trade Landmark: The Century-Long Transformation of the Hankou Alexander Nevsky Church
articles.abstract: 本文以武汉现存唯一的东正教建筑——汉口阿列克桑德聂夫堂（亚历山大·涅夫斯基教堂）为研究对象，系统梳理了其自1876年草创、历经晚清“东方茶港”繁荣、民国常态化发展直至建国后高度式微的百年历史变迁。文章结合实地考察，深入探讨了该建筑在2013年依托中俄“万里茶道”地缘历史叙事重获抢救性修缮的风貌复原过程。同时，作者指出，在当下的世俗化利用与展览叙事中，当局呈现出一种既渴望吸纳历史建筑的外交红利、又刻意回避其本源宗教属性与制度化衰落历史的矛盾心态。本研究不仅丰富了近代通商口岸异质信仰群体的微观历史，也为审视当代历史遗产保护中的意识形态焦虑与话语置换提供了参考。 Taking the Alexander Nevsky Church, the only surviving Orthodox architectural heritage in Wuhan, as the research object, this paper systematically delineates its century-long historical evolution, tracing its origins in 1876, its flourishing period during the late Qing Dynasty when Hankou served as the "Oriental Tea Port," its regularized development during the Republican era, and its post-1949 institutional decline. Based on field observations, the study examines the facade restoration process initiated in 2013, which was driven by the geopolitical and historical narrative of the Sino-Russian "Great Tea Road." Furthermore, the author points out a nuanced paradox in the contemporary secular utilization and exhibition narratives of the property: the authorities eagerly embrace the diplomatic dividends and cultural prestige of the historic building, while deliberately avoiding its fundamental religious attributes and the complex history of its institutional decline. This study not only enriches the microhistory of heterogeneous religious groups in modern treaty ports, but also provides empirical insights into ideological anxieties and discourse displacement in contemporary historical heritage conservation.

articles.title: Great Expectations? Researchers in Germany are Optimistic about the Potential of Grant Lotteries.
articles.abstract: In this study I investigate researchers’ expectations towards the potential advantages of grant lotteries in a representative sample of scientists at German universities and higher education institutions provided by the Scientists Survey of the German Centre for Higher Education Research and Science Studies (DZHW). I describe the saliency of the two debates on bias in grant peer review and on grant lotteries, as well as researchers’ levels of experience with grant peer review. I use both descriptive statistics and analytical models to investigate which characteristics shape scientists’ relative grant lottery optimism. I find that experienced and more senior scientists are significantly less optimistic about grant lotteries. Saliency and reviewer workload are positively associated with optimism. I conclude that, even though saliency of the issue remains sparse, researchers are generally optimistic about grant lotteries, yet also aware of some of their potential disadvantages.

articles.title: Individual perception of bias in grant peer review strongly associated with openness towards the introduction of lotteries.
articles.abstract: This study of a representative sample of scientists at German universities and higher education institutions investigates researchers’ individual perception of bias in grant peer review and their openness towards the potential introduction of grant lotteries, as well as the potential link between the two concepts. Indeed, bias in peer review is often cited in the theoretical debate on grant lotteries. But even though researchers are both very involved in and strongly affected by grant decision-making, there is not enough empirical evidence on their perspective. I find that bias perception is very prevalent, openness is generally rare and researchers who perceive more bias in grant peer review are more open towards grant lotteries in a substantial and statistically significant way.

articles.title: Domestic Peace Deficit: A Conceptual Framework for Understanding Gender-Based Violence through Institutional, Relational, and Structural Peace Failures

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Gender-based violence (GBV) continues to persist at high levels despite decades of legal reform, policy intervention, and scholarly attention. Existing approaches, drawn from criminology, public health, sociology, psychology, and law, have generated important insights into individual acts, risk factors, and immediate responses. Yet they remain less equipped to explain the cumulative institutional conditions that allow harm within domestic and intimate life to endure across the life course. This paper introduces the Domestic Peace Deficit (DPD) as a conceptual framework that addresses this gap. DPD explains how cumulative institutional failures undermine peace within domestic life by shaping exposure to violence, access to protection, and recognition of harm. Its central contribution is to treat the household as a peace system rather than merely a private social space or a site of interpersonal violence. Drawing on and extending insights from structural violence, positive peace, feminist peace research, human security, the ecological model of GBV, and intersectionality, the framework organises analysis around three pillars: the Violence and Coercion Deficit, the Agency and Relational Peace Deficit, and the Institutional and Structural Support Deficit. The paper defines domestic peace, formalises the deficit concept, outlines core principles, describes how the framework was developed, sketches pathways of accumulation, a future measurement agenda, and states the framework's principal limitations. DPD does not replace existing theories; it integrates and extends them into a coherent architecture centred on the domestic sphere. In doing so, it offers researchers, policymakers, and practitioners a tool for understanding why formal protections so often fail to produce lived safety, and for designing responses that address institutional recognition, accountability, and the intergenerational transmission of harm.

articles.title: Identity Claims in Political Speech
articles.authors: Asli Ceren Cinar, Mirya Holman, Tyler Simko
articles.abstract: Social identities shape political behavior, but when, how, and why do people talk about these identities? We introduce the concept of identity claiming: publicly identifying oneself as a member of a social group to establish standing and strengthen political appeals. Drawing on five corpora of political communication, including congressional newsletters, campaign biographies, social media, and public comments at school board and city council meetings, we show that elites and members of the public regularly make identity claims. The identities they invoke are not random: claims match the setting, deserving reference groups are used more frequently, and identity claims associated with increased vocal pitch. Experimental and social media evidence shows that speech with identity claims prompts engagement from the audience. Our work shows how ordinary people and political elites strategically and frequently engage in identity politics in their public communication.

articles.title: Das gelesene Buch. Lesen und Geschmackspräferenzen in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz
articles.authors: Carolin Amlinger, Luca Keiser, Oliver Nachtwey, Jörg Rössel
articles.abstract: This preprint presents descriptive findings from a standardised online survey on book reading conducted in Germany, Austria and Switzerland in May and June 2026 (N = 6,427; quota-sampled by gender, age, region and education). It asks how reading practices and literary preferences are socially distributed across the German-speaking countries. The findings suggest that what divides the reading public is not how much is read but whether people read at all: the share of avid readers varies only between 5 and 13 per cent across social groups, whereas the share of non-readers ranges from 7 to 30 per cent. Education marks the sharpest boundary, with the decisive break falling between the highly educated and everyone else rather than along a continuous gradient. Gender and having been read to in childhood operate as independent axes, while age structures taste more than volume. Evaluative criteria follow the same logic: immersion and involvement dominate across all groups, but formal criteria such as stylistic quality and complexity gain weight with education. At the same time, the cultural legitimacy of the book remains broadly acknowledged, including among those who barely read. The analysis is deliberately descriptive and serves as a first step towards subsequent multivariate analyses of the social and literary space.

articles.title: Support and contestation under the radar: How states promote and undermine the international fight against corruption

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This article investigates hidden forms of support for and contestation of international norms. Existing research largely focuses on publicly visible behavioural forms of contestation, such as member states’ exit from international organizations (IOs). However, less visible practices can also effectively undermine and sabotage international norms, or, conversely, strengthen them. We explore this phenomenon by researching a prominent IO in the global fight against corruption, the Group of States against Corruption (GRECO), by means of interviews with delegates to GRECO and members of the Council of Europe secretariat, complemented with an analysis of policy documents. The empirical evidence reveals five distinct types of hidden contestation and two types of hidden support. Contestation typically originates from the political macro-level rather than from the involved expert community. Member states contest GRECO’s authority through ineffective implementation, delays, obstructive voting, and by negotiating review outcomes. Conversely, peer pressure and peer support emerge as meaningful micro-level practices of norm support that counteract contestation. This study’s insights advance research on contestation and support of international norms and inform research, theory, and practice on how to strengthen the global fight against corruption.

articles.title: A Healthier Start Abroad? The health at birth of the children of migrants and of those born at origin
articles.abstract: The health of migrants is mostly studied in relation to destination-country natives, Origin-country comparisons are rarely pursued, even though they provide a more convincing counterfactual, allowing us to (a) measure “health gains” from migration, (b) disentangle mechanisms including selectivity, cultural factors and contextual change, (c) elucidate the relationship between migration and global health inequality. We address this gap by comparing the health at birth of children born in Spain to migrant parents from 15 origin countries with that of children born in those same origin countries, using Spanish vital statistics linked to Demographic and Health Surveys and other origin-country sources. We find that, for most groups, the children of migrants are healthier at birth (measured via low birth weight) than children in their parents' origin countries. This is also true among groups disadvantaged relative to Spanish natives, and is more pronounced for non-Western and, especially, Asian-origin groups. We find limited support for cultural explanations and stronger support for both migrant selectivity and improved contextual conditions at destination. Though the latter two are not fully separable, our evidence favors the effect of the change in contextual conditions. These results suggest migration can function as an equalizing force, narrowing birthplace-based health inequalities.

articles.title: When Resources Are Scarce: Formal Mentoring as a Compensatory Resource for Sustainable Performance Expectations
articles.abstract: Drawing on Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) theory, this study conceptualizes formal mentoring as a resource system and examines how mentoring functions, job resources and demands, self-empowerment, and organizational support relate to mentoring program effectiveness and sustainable performance expectations. Using cross-sectional self-report data from 71 participants in a formal peer mentoring program, we found that perceived program effectiveness was positively associated with sustainable performance expectations, defined as participants’ beliefs about their ability to sustain performance and well-being over time. Mentoring functions were positively related to program effectiveness and, indirectly, to sustainable performance expectations via perceived mentoring effectiveness. In addition, job cognitive resources, self-empowerment, and organizational support moderated the relationship between mentoring functions and program effectiveness, such that mentoring functions were most strongly associated with perceived effectiveness when these resources were lower. These findings suggest that mentoring functions may operate as compensatory resources in resource-constrained contexts. Employment status was also relevant, with full-time employed participants reporting higher program effectiveness than solopreneurs. Overall, the findings extend JD-R theory by positioning mentoring not only as a developmental intervention but also as a resource that supports sustainable human performance.

articles.title: Standardising Access to Digital Platform Data: A Taxonomy for Social Research
articles.authors: Futoon Abushaqra, Damiano Spina, Amanda Lawrence, Daniel Angus, Robert Glasgow
articles.abstract: [This manuscript has been submitted for peer review] Abstract: Recent regulations granting individuals the right to access their personal data stored on digital platforms have reshaped the landscape of data collection. Under frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in the European Union and the 2019 New York SHIELD Act, platforms are now required to provide users with mechanisms to retrieve and inspect their own data; commonly referred to as Data Download Packages (DDPs). These developments have enabled new forms of data collection through data donation, where users voluntarily share their DDPs for research purposes. However, the structure, format, and granularity of DDPs vary significantly across platforms and over time, posing challenges for researchers, especially those without technical expertise. Responding to these challenges, this paper contributes to the Australian Internet Observatory's broader agenda of building national research infrastructure for independent, public-interest platform research. We propose a taxonomy for categorising DDPs across different platforms, alongside a schema repository that systematically describes the content of each DDP, including its structure, data types, and formats. These contributions support a more consistent and comprehensive understanding of DDPs across diverse platforms, with a particular focus on social media and digital services, and enable their effective use in both academic and applied research contexts.

articles.title: Tracking Change, Informing Policy: Longitudinal Evidence of Shifting Political Affiliations and Public Attitudes Toward Higher Education
articles.authors: Stephen M Gavazzi, Suzanne Bartle-Haring, E. Gordon Gee
articles.abstract: This longitudinal study examines how public attitudes toward U.S. public higher education shifted between 2021 and 2025 across five policy-relevant domains: funding priorities, rural-urban engagement, global-local emphasis, financial aid preferences, and the perceived importance of national rankings. Using data from panel respondents across nine states, results show growing support for balanced approaches to geographic engagement, financial aid, and global-local activities, alongside increased prioritization of teaching and declining support for community engagement. Nearly 30 percent of participants changed their political affiliation over the four year period, and these shifts were strongly associated with changes in funding preferences, especially allocations to teaching. Cross lag analyses further indicate that changes in funding priorities, engagement emphases, and ideological self-placement help explain trust in state universities. Findings underscore the importance of longitudinal designs for understanding how individual-level political dynamics shape public expectations for, and confidence in, higher education.

articles.title: New alternatives, same orders: modern alternative proteins did not replace meat purchases in restaurants
articles.authors: Jared Winslow, Jacob Robert Peacock, Jayisha Dhargawe, Hailey Sherman, Seth Ariel Green, Maya Mathur
articles.abstract: Plant-based alternative proteins are widely expected to displace meat consumption and, in turn, reorient the global food system away from the externalities of animal agriculture, but little empirical work has assessed these presumed substitution effects in naturalistic settings. Here, we use a dataset of 1.2 million transactions across seven restaurants and eight years to investigate whether introducing modern alternative proteins to restaurant menus reduces purchases of meat-containing dishes. We analyzed effects on total meat purchases and on category-matched purchases, pairing each alternative protein with the meat it emulates; we also estimate individual (within-customer) purchasing changes. Our results from 40 preregistered outcome-exposure pairings are overwhelmingly null, whether pooled across restaurants or stratified by restaurant. These findings challenge the widespread belief that alternative proteins displace meat purchases.

articles.title: Digital state capacity: a conceptualization approach

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Digital technologies matter more and more for state affairs, yet few formulations define what digital is for the continuous structure of the state after decades of digitalization. This article argues that digital has become an essential dimension of state capacity. Drawing on an ontological-semantic approach to concept building, it constructs the concept of digital capacity around three necessary dimensions: digital apparatus, digital space control and digital interaction. It then develops the Digital Capacity Index, covering the 193 United Nations members from 2001 to 2022. Validity tests show a consistent concept-measure relationship and support comparative policy analysis of the digital state.

articles.title: Two Cycles, Not One: A Continuous-Time Point-Process Analysis of Reciprocal Violence in the Israeli–Palestinian Conflict

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Whether violence in the Israeli–Palestinian conflict is reciprocal — each side's lethal action provoking the other's — has been studied largely through vector-autoregression on time-binned counts, an approach that obscures the timing, branching structure, and directionality of response. We model lethal violence in the two directions as a bivariate Hawkes process, a continuous-time self- and mutually-exciting point process, using individual-incident fatality records from the Second Intifada through October 2023. Reciprocal excitation is genuine but profoundly asymmetric: a single Palestinian-to-Israeli event triggers on the order of one subsequent Israeli lethal event, nearly thirty times the reverse coupling. The asymmetry survives placebo, regime-detection, and flexible-baseline checks designed to rule out a common-driver confound, and goodness-of-fit testing confirms the models describe the data adequately. Allowing the couplings to take either sign, we find no evidence of deterrence in either direction. The strength of the Israeli response is statistically indistinguishable across the conflict's two main eras, but its speed is not: the characteristic response lag roughly halves between the Intifada and the later Gaza-war period, a temporal change binned methods cannot represent. Resolving the Israeli-to-Palestinian direction into its Gaza and West Bank theaters reveals that they operate as nearly independent systems: violence within each is strongly self-exciting while cross-theater coupling is negligible, and the reciprocal dynamic that dominates the pooled analysis is localized almost entirely to the West Bank, whereas Gaza's violence is driven by internal escalation. What appears in aggregate as a single cycle is, spatially, two barely-interacting logics — a separation we argue reflects the differential governance of the two territories rather than any natural division of the conflict. A three-stream extension shows settler violence to be a distinct channel: reactive to Palestinian action, increasingly self-exciting, and temporally preceding rather than following state violence. All findings replicate on an independently constructed event dataset. We document these regularities for 2000–2023 and set out why we do not extend them through the subsequent war: individual-incident records for that period exist, but not on a footing commensurable with the present analysis.

articles.title: The reach of violence: Infant health among diasporas in the United States during the onset of the 2023 Gaza War
articles.authors: Jasmin Abdel Ghany, Emma Romell, Joshua Wilde

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: A large body of research documents the harm that armed conflict inflicts on the health of populations in conflict zones. Yet if violence injures collectivities rather than only those who experience it directly, its health consequences should extend to those who identify with affected populations wherever they reside. We test this hypothesis by examining the effects of the October 7, 2023, attacks in Israel and the ensuing onset of the Gaza War on infant health in the United States among mothers born in Israel, the West Bank, and neighboring, Arab, and Muslim-majority countries. In a novel application of the event-study design, we trace month-by-month changes in preterm birth and low birthweight – outcomes that shape health and socioeconomic attainment throughout the life course. Our analyses show that the Israel-born diaspora experienced an immediate, short-lived reversal in their previously substantial infant health advantage after the October 7 attacks. Infant health also deteriorated among mothers born in neighboring, other Arab, and other Muslim-majority countries. These findings indicate that the health consequences of violence are not confined to the conflict zone but extend to geographically distant diaspora communities who are connected to the affected populations by shared national and ethnic origin and religion.

articles.title: Rethinking Social Sustainability Metrics in Chile’s Lithium Sociotechnical Transition: Numbers, Policies and Knowledge
articles.authors: Sebastián Herrera-León, Iván Ojeda-Pereira, Fernando Campos-Medina, Rodrigo Molina-Richardson
articles.abstract: Social sustainability indicators are central decision-support tools in mining, used to evaluate social performance and guide policy and investment. However, these indicators do not merely describe reality; they actively shape it by defining what is measured, reported, and governed. In the context of lithium extraction from brines, this performative role becomes particularly relevant as expanding production and technological changes reconfigure water use, territorial relations, and community livelihoods in sensitive ecosystems such as the high-Andean salt flats of Chile, which host some of the world's largest lithium reserves and production sites. This paper analyses how social sustainability is currently measured in the lithium industry and identifies the opportunities and limitations of existing indicator frameworks. Using a systematic analysis of sustainability reports and international reporting standards, combined with insights from stakeholder interviews, we examine the indicators commonly used to assess lithium extraction activities. The results show that existing indicator systems are structured by global reporting standards and compliance-oriented metrics, whilst territorial dynamics and relational aspects of social sustainability remain partially captured. Based on these results, the paper discusses implications for the design of social sustainability indicators in critical mineral extraction. We argue that improving sustainability assessment requires incorporating territorially situated perspectives, ecosystem-based knowledge, and broader participation of communities, universities, public institutions, and firms. In this sense, redesigning sustainability indicators as more reflexive and participatory tools may support more socially robust pathways in the sociotechnical transition of the lithium industry in Chile.

articles.title: Capitalizing on Controversy: Humor, Scandal Entrepreneurship, and the Rise of the Far Right
articles.abstract: Right-wing public figures, from comedians to politicians, increasingly use humor strategically to provoke scandal. While scandals are typically understood to damage the reputations of norm transgressors, the rise of successful right-wing scandal makers challenges this assumption. In this article, we introduce the concept of ‘scandal entrepreneur’ to theorize the rise of celebrity figures who deliberately create or amplify scandals for personal or political gain. Integrating insights from political scandal research, sociological work on cultural and moral entrepreneurship, and critical humor studies, we develop an innovative approach to scandal that combines dramaturgical and conjunctural analysis. Drawing on a quantitative mapping of Dutch humor scandals between 1990 and 2024 and an in-depth qualitative analysis of two cases, we trace both the steep rise in humor scandals in the early twenty-first century and the increasing professionalization of scandal entrepreneurship, which has turned scandal-making into a profitable business model. Based on our analysis of the Nekschot cartoon scandal (2008) and the VI-Akwasi scandal (2020), we demonstrate that, within the current cultural conjuncture, right-wing actors are best positioned to capitalize on scandals and successfully dramatize social and cultural divides through humor. Our approach offers valuable analytical tools for humor and scandal scholarship and the field of right-wing studies, providing a critical lens through which to examine wider cultural changes.

articles.title: AI Parasocial Relationships and The Potential Role of Miswanting in Loneliness and Emotional Distress: A Theoretical Review
articles.abstract: The evolution of artificial intelligence has led to the development of more advanced AI systems that can create human like conversation. This increases the usage of AI chatbots into sources of social interaction, emotional support, and companionship. Recent researches have examined their potential benefits and risk but less attention has been given to the individuals expectations regarding the emotional benefits of artificial intelligence. The present theoretical review proposes miswanting as a central theme for understanding the discrepancy between anticipated and actual emotional fulfilment in human- AI relationship. Drawing upon the theories of miswanting, parasocial relationship, self-determination and loneliness theories this review highlights the conceptual framework linking pre-existing loneliness and unmet emotional needs to AI companion use, emotional attachment, expectations of fulfilment, and subsequent psychological outcomes. The framework proposes that individuals may initially experience AI companionship as emotionally comforting and socially supportive and develops expectations that such interaction can satisfy long term emotional and relatedness needs. When experienced outcomes don’t match with these expectations, an expectation- reality discrepancy occurs which may eventually lead to persistent loneliness, emotional. Importantly, the framework does not assume that AI companionship is inherently harmful; rather, it highlights the potential importance of miswanting theory to the emerging context of AI companionship. This review offers a novel conceptual perspective and generates testable propositions for future empirical research.

articles.title: "It's Just About Being with My Friends": Children's Perspectives on the Use, Risks and Benefits of Virtual Worlds Platforms
articles.abstract: Despite the central role that virtual worlds based on user-generated content, such as Roblox, play in the digital lives of children and adolescents, research incorporating their first-hand experiences and perspectives of these platforms remains limited. Roblox is one of the world's largest virtual world platforms, used predominantly by children and adolescents, with most users estimated to be under the age of 16. Grounded in a children's rights perspective, this study adopts an arts-based qualitative approach that combines cognitive mapping through drawing with follow-up interviews to explore what children's and adolescents' perceptions of Roblox reveal about its risks and benefits. To address this aim, we engaged 29 children aged 10–16 in partnership with an international school in Italy. Our analysis identifies three key findings with theoretical and regulatory implications. First, rather than simply as a game, participants perceive and use Roblox primarily as a social platform where they play and communicate with friends, form new relationships, and maintain long-distance connections. Related to that, participants also perceive Roblox as operating in ways that resemble social media platforms. Second, these social dynamics are closely intertwined with risks, including exposure to scams, toxic interactions, grooming, online dating practices, and monetisation pressures. Third, participants routinely migrate to platforms such as Discord and WhatsApp for communication, circumventing Roblox's age-based restrictions and complicating platform-specific safeguarding efforts. These findings highlight the need for adaptive safeguarding strategies and contribute to theoretical discussions of the increasingly blurred boundaries between digital games and social media and children’s online safety.

articles.title: Ambient Load and Human Dignity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Structural Stability Science (SSS) Briefing on Boundary, Load Displacement, and Institutional Responsibility
articles.abstract: This public-facing institutional briefing applies Structural Stability Science (SSS), Dimensional Human Field Theory (DHFT), the Structural Identification Method (SIM), and Load–Capacity–Boundary Mechanics (LCB) to a structural question raised by artificial intelligence and human dignity: when machine-mediated systems become more powerful, efficient, opaque, and difficult to contest, where does the Load go? The briefing identifies Ambient Load as non-decomposed Load remaining active as unresolved background demand under conditions of ambiguity, avoidance, unclear authority, unstable Boundary mediation, undefined terms, machine-mediated misclassification, or unlocated responsibility. It further identifies Load Displacement Through Ambiguity as a structural condition in which unresolved ambiguity transfers the burden of clarification, stabilization, correction, compliance, repair, or source preservation onto another actor or system layer. In the institutional context opened by Pope Leo XIV’s public teaching on artificial intelligence and the safeguarding of the human person, this briefing analyzes the convergence between a public moral-institutional concern and a structural-scientific classification problem. It does not provide legal, clinical, theological, compliance, technical AI, or engineering advice and does not authorize use of SSS, DHFT, SIM, LCB, Ambient Load, Structural Drift, or related source architecture for assessment, audit, certification, training, institutional deployment, machine use, implementation, or derivative method development. Technical Note: This record is a public-facing Structural Stability Science briefing. It applies the SSS / DHFT / SIM / LCB source architecture to an institutional question concerning artificial intelligence, human dignity, Ambient Load, Boundary degradation, Load coupling, and Load displacement. It does not replace, modify, or expand the DHFT source architecture and does not authorize assessment, audit, certification, training, implementation, machine use, or derivative method development.
