articles.title: Assessment of Broadcast Regulation Patterns in Nigeria
articles.authors: Adriel Ekozin, Hussain Bin Hyacinth, Prof. Abigail Odozi Ogwezzy-Ndisika, Olunifesi Adekunle Suraj
articles.abstract: This paper examined the major patterns of broadcast regulation in Nigeria, their operational dynamics and implications for professionalism, accountability and broadcast media freedom. Through the lens of Social Responsibility Theory, the paper conceptualised broadcast regulation as a multi-layered system comprising self-regulation, internal regulation, statutory regulation and co-regulation. A qualitative case study design was adopted, with data generated through semi-structured interviews involving 15 purposively selected broadcast experts and scholars. The data were analysed using thematic analysis. Findings showed that broadcast regulation in Nigeria operates through a combination of individual professional responsibility, organisational control mechanisms, statutory oversight by the National Broadcasting Commission (NBC) and stakeholder participation in regulatory processes. The paper further found that licensing procedures, compliance with Nigeria Broadcasting Code, consultations and enforcement constitute the major operational frameworks of regulation. However, political interference, selective enforcement and the limited autonomy of the NBC emerged as significant challenges. While the regulatory system contributes to professionalism and accountability, concerns regarding ownership influence, regulatory bias and excessive government involvement were found to undermine broadcast media freedom and audience confidence in the regulatory process. The paper concluded that effective broadcast regulation in the country requires a balanced integration of self-regulation, internal regulation, statutory regulation and co-regulation. It, therefore, recommended strengthening the institutional independence of the NBC to ensure fair, transparent and credible regulation capable of promoting both professional standards and broadcast media freedom.

articles.title: Mass Media Agenda Setting Role and the Fight against Crude Oil Theft in Bayelsa State, Nigeria
articles.authors: Adriel Ekozin, Beatrice Okatubo Manasseh, Ezekiel S. Asemah
articles.abstract: This study examined how the mass media can contribute to efforts aimed at curtailing crude oil theft in Bayelsa State. The paper was anchored on the agenda setting theory as its theoretical framework, while library research method was adopted as its methodology. The paper discovered that the role of the media in curbing crude oil theft is connected to their functions of informing, educating and entertaining society. The paper concluded that the media can assist in combating crude oil theft by giving prominence to the issue and portraying its negative impact on Nigeria, the state, actors and communities. It recommended that the media, especially, radio should increase the amount of time given to the coverage of crude oil theft.

articles.title: Influencers Credibility and Consumer Purchase Decision across Cultures
articles.authors: Adriel Ekozin, Victoria Ukwuamedua, Faith Ozikor Amah
articles.abstract: This study examined the influence of influencer credibility on consumer purchase decisions across cultures. It looked at how trustworthiness, expertise, authenticity and relatability of social media influencers shape consumers’ willingness to accept product recommendations and make purchase decisions in different cultural contexts. The study is based on the source credibility theory. The study adopts a library research methodology, drawing on existing scholarly works, textbooks and journal articles on influencer marketing, consumer behaviour and cross-cultural communication. Findings from the reviewed literature show that influencer credibility plays a significant role in shaping consumer trust and purchase intentions. However, its influence varies across cultures due to differences in values, communication styles and perceptions of authenticity. In some cultural settings, consumers prioritise expertise and professionalism, while in others, relatability and lifestyle similarity are more important. The study further reveals that although credible influencers can increase consumer engagement and purchase intention, other factors such as cultural orientation, peer influence and personal preferences also affect final purchase decisions. The study concluded that influencer credibility is a strong but culturally dependent determinant of consumer purchase behaviour. It recommended that influencers maintain authenticity and transparency, and that brands consider cultural alignment when selecting influencers for marketing campaigns.

articles.title: Exploring News Consumption Patterns of Female Digital Natives in Abuja
articles.authors: Adriel Ekozin, Akuta Michelle Idialu, Desmond Onyemechi Okocha, Fidelis Olarinde Olugbamiye
articles.abstract: The emergence of technology has given rise to a shift in the news consumption patterns of media audiences. This study examined the news consumption patterns of Nigeria’s female digital natives, focusing on their preferred media platforms, news interests, attitudes toward traditional and digital sources, and the influence of social media on their news consumption patterns. Guided by Uses and Gratifications and Technological Determinism theories, the study adopted a quantitative survey design, with a sample size of 176. Purposive and snowball sampling techniques were used. Using a structured questionnaire, data were collected from female digital natives in Abuja Municipal Area Council. The findings revealed a strong preference for digital platforms such as Instagram, driven by accessibility, interactivity and real-time updates. The findings also indicated that respondents had greater interest in soft news, such as entertainment and lifestyle, than in hard news, such as politics or business. The study further found that while female digital natives actively select news to satisfy personal needs, their habits are shaped by digital technologies and algorithmic structures. It therefore concluded that the behaviour of female digital natives represents a shift from passive consumption toward interactive, personalised and algorithmically mediated news experiences. The study recommends that traditional and online news outlets increase their presence and engagement on social media platforms where female digital natives are most active in order to enhance their growing interest in news consumption. The study further found that while female digital natives actively select news to satisfy personal needs, their habits are shaped by digital technologies and algorithmic structures. It therefore concluded that the behaviour of female digital natives represents a shift from passive consumption toward interactive, personalised and algorithmically mediated news experiences. The study recommends that traditional and online news outlets increase their presence and engagement on social media platforms where female digital natives are most active in order to enhance their growing interest in news consumption.

articles.title: Crossing Fields: Toward a Theory of Symbolic Portability in Chinese Creator Platform Migration
articles.abstract: Chinese digital creators move constantly between Douyin, Bilibili, and Xiaohongshu, three platforms that define creative worth in incompatible ways, yet platform migration has almost no theoretical home. Platform studies treats each platform as a closed environment; Bourdieusian applications to digital culture stay within a single platform or national ecosystem. Neither asks what happens to a creator's accumulated symbolic capital when it crosses a platform boundary. This paper develops symbolic portability: the conditional capacity of a creator's IP, an integrated system of persona, content, and narrative, to retain, partially retain, or lose recognition value when carried into a different platform field. Drawing on Bourdieu's field theory and Sinophone platform scholarship on state-directed platform capitalism, this paper builds a conceptual model linking recognition regimes, migration, capital conversion, and professional subjectivity, and argues that Chinese platform migration is a theoretically generative case largely invisible to Western single-platform studies.

articles.title: Special Grade Cursed Object: How Award Certificates Become Licenses for Organizational Domination
articles.abstract: This paper develops the concept of the “Special Grade Cursed Object” to explain how visible prizes such as award certificates, plaques, trophies, diplomas, credentials, and organizational honors can transform past recognition into present authority within organizations. These objects are not inherently harmful. In ordinary settings, they record effort, achievement, expertise, and institutional contribution. However, when they are repeatedly displayed in organizational space and become attached to a particular person’s position, past success, symbolic status, or the organization’s own evaluative judgment, they may begin to function as more than commemorative objects. They can become symbolic media that reduce criticizability, weaken upward feedback, and legitimize present domination. Drawing on research on symbolic capital, organizational artifacts, institutional legitimacy, psychological safety, organizational silence, abusive supervision, social learning, and prestige bias, this paper examines how a prize can shift from being a record of past achievement to becoming a license for present authority. An award certificate does not directly produce anger, intimidation, or domination. Yet when it strengthens the symbolic status of a particular person, coworkers may hesitate to express criticism, the organization may avoid questioning its previous evaluation, and the honored person may interpret current behavior as already justified by past achievement. In this process, harshness can be reframed as responsibility, intimidation as discipline, and silence as agreement. The paper also examines how anger protected by symbolic recognition can be imitated by others. The symbolic capital attached to an honored person cannot easily be copied, but the style of anger, public reprimand, labeling, and downward aggression can be reproduced. In this way, visible prizes may become media through which patterns of domination and emotional control are culturally transmitted within organizations. The argument is not that award certificates or trophies should be removed. Rather, the problem arises when past honor obscures present responsibility. To “de-curse” such objects is not to destroy them, but to return them to their proper role as records of past achievement and reconnect them with present accountability, feedback, and criticizability.

articles.title: Media and Public Opinion in Foreign Policy Making in Bangladesh
articles.abstract: The influence of the media in determining public opinion and informing foreign policy-making processes in Bangladesh is considerable. The media impacts decision-making indirectly, while also acting as a forum for information and public discussion, which affects foreign policy formulation and implementation. This study analyzes the nature of the relationship between media, public opinion, and foreign policy in Bangladesh through analyses of historical developments, theoretical concepts, and current practices. The study draws attention to the media's role in Bangladesh's Liberation War, national and international media's contributions, the development of the country's media landscape, and the rise of digital journalism and social media. Informed by insights from the CNN Effect, Al Jazeera Effect, and soft power, the study identifies the media's construction of narratives that influence public perceptions of Bangladesh's bilateral relations with India, China, Pakistan, and other regional actors. The paper further explores the media's contributions to track-two diplomacy, public diplomacy, and the development of Bangladesh's international image. It contends that media acts as a crucial middleman between policymakers and citizens, as it raises foreign policy awareness, fosters debates, and sways the degree of public backing of such diplomatic efforts. Despite issues with press freedom, regulation, and digital misinformation, media remains an essential constituent of Bangladesh's foreign policy context and a key tool in advancing national interests amid an ever-connected world.

articles.title: Always Look on the Bright Side of Work: Dignity Lighter as a Counter-Model to the Heart Slicer
articles.abstract: This paper proposes the concept of the Dignity Lighter as a counter-model to the Heart Slicer in workplace communication. The Heart Slicer Model explains how repeated micro-devaluation, public correction, labeling, silence, comparison, and avoidance gradually erode a worker’s self-understanding, capacity for voice, capacity for action, sense of belonging, and relational presence. In contrast, the Dignity Lighter refers to a person or communicative practice that recognizes another person’s real, observed, and specific strengths in a sincere manner, thereby restoring dignity, self-trust, capacity for voice, and capacity for action. The paper distinguishes Dignity Lighting from generic praise and instrumental praise. While instrumental praise uses compliment-like language for management, appeasement, or hierarchical stabilization, Dignity Lighting is grounded in authentic specific affirmation: the sincere recognition of a concrete strength actually observed in another person. The paper further introduces domain-transcending affirmation, in which abilities expressed outside the formal work domain, such as narrative skill, observation, explanation, prediction, or interpretive competence, are recognized and reconnected to workplace self-trust. A central argument of the paper is that sincere affirmation requires psychological security. A person whose self-esteem has been repeatedly eroded may lose the ability to recognize another person’s excellence without experiencing it as a threat. This condition is theorized as affirmation capacity collapse, in which genuine recognition is replaced by denial, comparison, devaluation, or labeling. Drawing on research on self-esteem, social comparison, social learning, psychological safety, self-determination theory, organizational silence, and micro-affirmations, the paper positions Dignity Lighting as a form of workplace repair. The paper argues that workplace repair does not begin only by prohibiting anger or stopping silence. It also requires the restoration of response, recognition, and dignity. If the Heart Slicer makes people smaller than their roles, the Dignity Lighter reminds people that they are larger than their roles. Dignity Lighting is therefore not mere kindness, optimism, or praise. It is a dignity-restoring communicative practice that interrupts the reproduction of workplace devaluation and helps recover agency, voice, and hidden competence.

articles.title: Female Gaze in Telugu cinema: A Visual Content Analysis of Nandhu Reddy’s oh! Baby (2019)
articles.abstract: Female gaze is a powerful and genuine way of seeing that has not been fully recognized or explored yet. Dissimilar to the male gaze Maggie (Nelson 2009). Telling authentic stories about women contributing the genuine voices to cinema rather than attempting the impossible(Meghie 2020) The popular quote of a Canadian filmmaker stands prominently that she says “I cannot represent everything to everyone — and neither do I want to. I represent women like me when I’m at my best and writing honestly,” The female gaze enables women to face the camera, and tell their own stories, and represent their bodies from their own perspective. Sanchez, D. (2022) this study challenges the female gaze by overseeing a comparative study of male and female characters portrayed in the film ‘oh! Baby’ (2019) by Nandu Reddy. The theoretical framework of female Gaze and Fluid Gaze are reinforced to extract feminine and masculine portrayal within the study. This study employs visual content analysis to critically examine the portrayal of the character in Oh! Baby (2019). It investigates how the female director’s perspective shapes the representation of womanhood, exploring themes of identity, agency, and societal norms through cinematic language. By focusing on a woman’s viewpoint behind the camera, the study aims to reveal nuanced dimensions of female character portrayal that challenge conventional gender stereotypes in Telugu cinema. This research contributes to broader discussions on female authorship and gender representation in regional Indian films.

articles.title: Domain-specific emotional effects of deepfakes on news-sharing behaviour
articles.authors: Kei Ichikawa, Jiayu Chen, Kazutoshi Sasahara
articles.abstract: The rise of generative AI has raised societal concerns about the potential of synthetic media or deepfakes for misinformation. While previous research has established that negative emotions drive text-based misinformation sharing, their influence on deepfake dissemination remains poorly understood. Through two online experiments (N=494; N=489), we examined how emotional valence in AI-generated news images (deepfakes) affects sharing intentions across political and entertainment news domains. Using GPT-3.5 Turbo and Stable Diffusion V1, we manipulated image emotional valence while maintaining consistent news contexts. Results revealed that negative images increased sharing intention only for political content, not entertainment content. Moreover, replacing negative images with less negative alternatives reduced sharing intention for political news, even among those initially inclined to share. These findings suggest domain-specific emotional dynamics in the sharing of synthetic news images and point to novel content moderation strategies based on affective computing.

articles.title: Dynamic Savings with Adaptive Adjustment in the Solow–Swan Model: Bistability and Escape from a Poverty Trap
articles.abstract: We extend the Solow–Swan growth model by replacing the constant savings rate with a savings rate that adjusts gradually toward a capital-dependent target of Hill form. The savings rate becomes a state variable, turning the model into a two-dimensional dynamical system. For a sufficiently savings steep target, the system admits a poverty-trap regime with three equilibria: the origin, a saddle, and a stable high-capital equilibrium. We characterize the stability of every positive equilibrium by the elasticity of the savings target; in the bistable phase portrait, the saddle’s stable manifold provides the natural separatrix between the two observed attraction regions. We then study escape by a temporary public-investment flow. A direct geometric argument identifies an upper forward-invariant region from which the uncontrolled system converges to the high-capital equilibrium. If the investment flow satisfies a sufficient condition, the policy drives capital above a buffer level in finite time; savings then catches up through adaptive adjustment, after which the stimulus can be removed permanently. The model therefore converts the one-dimensional threshold of a static savings specification into a two-dimensional basin problem, where both the level of capital and the speed of savings adjustment are necessary for escape.

articles.title: Humility in Journalism: The epistemic virtue that allows journalists to learn from experiences of others
articles.abstract: Journalists have long been associated with a strong ego and the hubris necessary to share the news as “the way it is.” But overlooked, and perhaps more important, is the humility required by journalists to gather new knowledge in the first place. Through the lens of joy and journalistic epistemology, the present study explores interviews with 27 journalists in Chile and the United States in regards to their experiences with humility. Journalists broadly believed that their work could be done without humility, but that good journalism necessitated humility. The best journalists, across these national contexts, were considered to be those who were humble: which journalists defined as being willing to listen, to learn, to be corrected and to apologize for mistakes.

articles.title: Do Large Language Models Reproduce Question-Wording Effects? A Type-Level Map from Published Split-Ballot Experiments
articles.abstract: Whether large language models (LLMs) can stand in for human survey respondents is contested: some studies report striking correspondence with human data, others report systematic failure. We argue the question is mis-posed as a binary and answer it instead with a type-level map. We assembled 56 experiment pairs from published split-ballot experiments in the Time-sharing Experiments for the Social Sciences (TESS) archive - verbatim condition wordings with condition-level response distributions computed from public raw data - spanning ten classic questionnaire-design manipulations in the Schuman-Presser tradition. LLM respondents were conditioned on demographic profiles sampled from each original study's own probability-sample respondents and answered one condition each (n = 300 per condition, three seeds), in a preregistered design with a fully disclosed pilot, same-item internal replication on new seeds, and a hash-locked corpus. Reproduction divided by effect type. Semantics-based effects - lexical wording, question form, and equivalency framing - moved in the human direction on 7 of 8 significant pairs; because those pairs cluster in four studies, cluster-robust tests leave this as a consistent pattern rather than a confirmed one (study-level permutation p = .13). On a common, range-standardized effect scale the semantic-family correlation is r = .32 (cluster-bootstrap CI [.05, .79]; Spearman rho = .58), with magnitudes attenuated to roughly one-fifth to one-third of the human effects. Cognitive-burden-based effects failed as mechanism predicts: forced-choice response-order effects were at chance (1 of 4), and a recall-instruction effect was flat. Two model-specific signatures emerged, each anchored in a single item pair: acquiescence to a socially undesirable assertion vanished (human effect +.39; LLM -.00; z = -7.8), a pattern consistent with alignment training, and the models over-acquiesced to contradictory generic assertions (agreement sum 1.82 vs. .81 in humans). On six pilot-unexposed extension pairs, significant-pair signs matched in 5 of 6 model-pair evaluations across two models, which weakens simple literature-memorization accounts but cannot exclude pretraining exposure. We also document a mid-study behavioral discontinuity of a commercially served model under a stable model name, consistent with serving-version drift. Overall, the evidence supports an exploratory, direction-oriented use of LLM panels for pretesting semantic wording manipulations, and cautions against any use as a general-purpose effect estimator.

articles.title: Hype as a Critique of Communication: What Exaggeration Costs, Seen Through Five Lenses
articles.abstract: Calling something hype is a charge against communication. Yet it rarely specifies the fault. Was the claim inaccurate, oversold, over-promised, or crowding out something more deserving? Different lenses of communication theory show different faults, and different remedies. Exaggeration buys reach, assent, uptake, frame dominance, and resonance, often several at once. What differs is the cost. Read as information transfer, exaggeration spends the discriminating power of language; as rhetoric, the credibility of the speaker and their peers; as a speech act, the coordinating force of commitment and assertion; as discourse, the space in which opposing views can be uttered and acknowledged; as a pattern of reception, the contestability of a social representation held in common. These are over-generalization, over-selling, over-commitment, over-shadowing, and over-resonance. None requires intention. A field can overshoot through contributions that are individually calibrated and sincere, and where speakers relinquish control over reception, hype becomes a matter of platform design and power. Each lens is blind to what the others register, and a remedy reaches only those positioned to apply it.

articles.title: Backlash and the Limits of Immigrant Solidarity
articles.abstract: Does anti-immigrant backlash unite the people it targets? Using Cooperative Election Study data from 2010--2025, we track the pro-immigration attitudinal gradient, from third-generation US-born respondents to noncitizens, through Donald Trump's rise. The gradient contracted and remained smaller afterward; the fully adjusted 2010--2024 estimate is a 0.133-SD reduction from third-generation US-born respondents to noncitizens. Recurring items show why: third-generation respondents liberalized more, while naturalized citizens moved modestly toward restriction on conditional legalization. The contraction appears both on policies governing new immigration and on policies affecting immigrants already present, survives timing, measurement, composition, local-context, and unrelated-outcome checks, and is smaller among immigrants with longer residential tenure, homeownership, and higher income. Republican and conservative immigrants also shift less---not more---than simple cue-taking predicts. Backlash can make a category politically salient without making the people associated with it more politically aligned.

articles.title: Exploring socioeconomic inequalities in healthy and sustainable diets using big data: An observational analysis of loyalty card data from a UK Retailer, 2022.
articles.authors: Mark Alan Green, Emma Wilkins, Mark Gilthorpe, Thomas Sawczuk, Charlotte Hardman, Hannah Greatwood, Rebecca Ann Stone, Alexandra Johnstone, Michelle Morris

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Introduction: Promoting healthier and more sustainable diets is needed to improve population and planetary health. However, limited evidence has described how these intersecting issues vary together by socioeconomic position. Our study uses novel large-scale retailer consumer purchase data, adjusted for known biases, to explore socioeconomic inequalities in health and environmental impacts of food and beverage purchases. Methods: Data were household-level loyalty card records from a major UK supermarket retailer between 24th July and 31st December 2022 (n = 117 710). The health-related outcome was proportion of purchases that were ‘High in Fat, Salt or Sugar’ (HFSS), determined using the UK nutrient profile model. We estimated three environmental outcomes: total greenhouse gas emissions, total land use footprint, and total water use from food purchases. Multilevel regression with post-stratification was used to estimate each outcome measure by level of neighbourhood socioeconomic deprivation, adjusted for age, household size, distance to nearest supermarket, and urbanicity. We also described environmental outcomes by food category across level of deprivation. Results: Households residing in the most deprived 10% of areas purchased a larger proportion of HFSS items than households in the least deprived 10% of areas. Households in the least deprived 10% of areas had a greater absolute environmental impact. However, when considered per weight of items, households in the most deprived 10% of areas purchased items that contributed to higher greenhouse emissions per kg but had lower impacts for land use. Soft drinks, ready meals, pasta, and pastry products were identified as key food categories for targeted ‘food swaps’ to reduce environmental inequalities. Conclusions: Our novel application of retailer loyalty card data shows how these data can offer valuable insights for informing strategies to promote healthy, sustainable, and equitable diets. Tackling environmental inequalities in food purchases requires tailoring approaches to different population groups.

articles.title: Additional evidence on Madagascar's tourism-led growth hypothesis
articles.abstract: We evaluate the validity of the tourism-led growth (TLG) hypothesis for Madagascar through an examination of the asymmetric relationships among economic growth, tourism activity, and financial development over the period 2007Q1-2024Q4. Nonlinear Autoregressive Distributed Lag (NARDL) modeling reveals a statistically significant long-run asymmetric effect, wherein negative shocks to tourist arrivals exert a stronger adverse impact on economic growth than the expansionary effect of equivalent increases. With respect to causal dynamics, bivariate symmetric Granger causality testing first uncovers empirical support for the TLG hypothesis. Subsequent short-run asymmetric causality then supports the conservation hypothesis, wherein negative economic growth shocks trigger positive tourist inflows. This dynamic suggests that tourism functions as a counter-cyclical shock absorber during domestic downturns. Consequently, our analysis highlights the need to pivot strategy away from mere tourist volume toward high-yield retention and investment in a resilient tourism sector.

articles.title: Cognitive Degradation: The Reconfiguration of the Labor Process and Knowledge Authority in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly entering knowledge-intensive work, including programming, writing, design, analysis, and management. Unlike earlier forms of automation that were often concentrated on physical operations or clearly defined executional tasks, generative AI can produce text, code, classifications, and proposals within the workflow itself. Its significance therefore lies not simply in the displacement of particular tasks, but in the possibility that activities once associated with professional judgment become increasingly mediated by corporate technological systems. This paper examines that possibility through the concept of “cognitive degradation.” Drawing on Marx’s analysis of machinery and fixed capital, Braverman’s account of labor-process control and deskilling (Braverman, 1974), and Burawoy’s emphasis on worker agency and consent (Burawoy, 1978; 1979), the paper defines cognitive degradation narrowly. It occurs when AI takes over cognitive tasks previously performed by workers, workers’ effective authority over the criteria and application of judgment declines, and that shift is stabilized through organizational rules, technological systems, or labor institutions. The concept therefore should not be treated as synonymous with deskilling, declining productivity, or algorithmic management. To explore the mechanism, the paper examines three ideal types rather than three directly comparable causal cases: boundary-setting in the Writers Guild of America (WGA), internalization in AI-assisted software development, and institutional mediation through German co-determination. The cases show that AI can increase productivity without necessarily reducing workers’ skills, while still altering how knowledge and judgment are organized. The paper argues that the central issue in AI-mediated labor is therefore not whether machines replace workers, but whether workers retain meaningful authority over the definition, evaluation, and application of knowledge. The paper further proposes that sustained changes in such authority may affect occupational autonomy, skill formation, and bargaining power. Claims about macro-level class restructuring, however, remain propositions for future empirical research rather than conclusions established by the cases examined here.

articles.title: Are environmental and climate worries connected to individual feelings of anomie? Evidence from the German Socio-Economic Panel Study
articles.abstract: Feelings of anomie manifest themselves in perceptions of meaninglessness and disorientation that are expected to arise in response to rapid social change and threatening social conditions. We analyze whether and how concerns about environmental protection and the impacts of climate change (“environmental worries”) contribute to individual feelings of anomie, based on theoretically informed hypotheses about distinct relationships across social class. Fixed-effects panel regression and random intercept cross-lagged models are used, based on data from the German Socioeconomic Panel study (GSOEP; years 2008–2023). We find that environmental worries contribute to feelings of anomie but are trumped by adverse events in individual’s life course. The contribution of environmental worries to feelings of anomie is weak compared to worries about one’s own economic situation and health. Levels of both, feelings of anomie and environmental worries, are relatively stable within individuals across the years, whereas spill-over effects between the two are seldom observed. Exclusively in the social class of lower-grade professionals a positive spill-over effect of anomie on environmental worries is observed, whereas among blue-collar workers a negative connection is found. The findings are discussed regarding their contribution to a theory-driven explanation of how climate change and environmental degradation might promote social disintegration.

articles.title: Beyond the Deepfake: Synthetic Persuasion and the Infrastructural Transformation of Political Communication
articles.abstract: Political communication research has approached deepfakes primarily as deceptive audiovisual artifacts whose democratic relevance depends on realism, detection, and the possibility of misleading citizens. This perspective remains necessary but is increasingly insufficient. Generative artificial intelligence now enables political actors and intermediaries to produce, adapt, personalize, and recirculate persuasive text, image, audio, video, and conversational content at a scale that exceeds the conventional deepfake problem. This article develops the concept of synthetic persuasion to describe political influence processes in which AI-generated, AI-transformed, or AI-assisted symbolic content is deliberately embedded in communicative strategies designed to shape attention, interpretation, evaluation, identity, trust, or behavior. Building on a focused theory-building synthesis of research on deepfakes, political persuasion, platformization, algorithmic visibility, fact-checking, and AI governance, the article proposes the Synthetic Persuasion Infrastructure (SPI) model. The model distinguishes four analytically connected stages: production, platform embedding, amplification, and reception-recirculation. It argues that the political power of synthetic content cannot be reduced to successful deception: persuasion may also operate through narrative congruence, repetition, identity reinforcement, uncertainty, strategic disclosure, and hybrid-media amplification. Six propositions translate the model into falsifiable expectations for future comparative and experimental research. The article concludes that the democratic challenge posed by generative AI lies less in the existence of isolated synthetic objects than in the emergence of infrastructures capable of producing and circulating persuasive variants continuously across platforms and publics.

articles.title: NursingWave: entry, exit, and market concentration of home-visit nursing providers across Japan's secondary medical zones, 2020–2026

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Background: Japan's home-visit nursing workforce faces the most acute shortage of any nursing field, and national policy deliberations moved in July 2026 from prefecture-level to secondary-medical-zone-level data. Existing evidence, however, consists of static cross-sections; the dynamics of the provider market have never been measured at zone level. Methods: We constructed a semiannual panel of all home-visit nursing providers listed in the national long-term care information disclosure registry across 12 waves (December 2020 to June 2026), linked providers by insurance provider number, and assigned them to 330 secondary medical zones using a bitemporal municipality-to-zone crosswalk. We computed supply density per population aged 75+, cumulative entry/exit rates, turnover, corporate-group market concentration (HHI), and physician-issued home-visit nursing instructions (NDB item C007) per zone, with Theil decomposition of inequality. All sources are open data; the dataset, code, and an interactive viewer are released under CC BY 4.0. Results: Providers grew 41.5% nationally (13,032 to 18,436), with designated stations up 48.4% and deemed medical institutions down 16.7%. Yet 43 of 330 zones (13.0%) experienced net decline, concentrated in small zones (24.3% of zones with <25,000 residents aged 75+ vs. 1.7% of large zones), which also showed 12-fold higher market concentration (median HHI 0.125 vs. 0.010). Within-prefecture disparities accounted for 38.4% of total inequality. Same-name re-registrations explained only 2.1% of 5,729 observed exits. Conclusions: Behind aggregate growth, small zones face a triple disadvantage — lower density, net provider retreat, and single-provider dependence — invisible in prefecture statistics. Zone-level dynamic monitoring is feasible with open data alone.

articles.title: Closing The Domestic Peace Gap Applying the Domestic Peace Deficit Framework to SDG 5, SDG 16, and the Women, Peace and Security Agenda

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Over the past three decades, the international community has adopted an unprecedented set of legal, policy, and institutional commitments to advance gender equality, protect women and girls from violence, and promote peaceful and inclusive societies, most notably through Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 5 and 16 and the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda. Yet global monitoring confirms that progress on the relevant targets remains off track, and everyday realities inside households continue to diverge sharply from these commitments. This paper argues that the principal barrier is not the absence of formal commitments but the limited capacity of institutions to translate those commitments into lived domestic security, a pattern it terms the domestic peace gap. It applies the Domestic Peace Deficit (DPD) framework, developed in a companion conceptual paper (Ezeukwu, 2026), as an implementation lens for SDG 5, SDG 16, and the four WPS pillars of Prevention, Protection, Participation, and Relief and Recovery. The paper maps DPD's three pillars against relevant SDG targets and WPS commitments, and closes with practical recommendations for governments, United Nations agencies and development partners, and civil society organisations. Its central contribution is diagnostic and practical rather than theoretical: it shows how an institutional-performance lens, rather than an institutional-presence lens, can be used to evaluate whether global commitments are producing safer households.

articles.title: Fugitive Statistics: A Verification-Chain Protocol for Preserving Policy Numbers That Exist Only Inside Documents

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: A growing share of policy-critical statistics is published only as tables embedded in advisory-committee documents — ad hoc tabulations produced for a single meeting, carried exclusively by PDF, with no versioned machine-readable release, no persistent identifier, and no documented reproduction path. We term these fugitive statistics, by analogy with the fugitive documents of library science — government publications that fall within the scope of a depository system yet escape its collection net. Fugitive statistics are load-bearing: they inform national workforce projections, capacity planning, and crisis-response policy, yet they are exposed to link rot, silent revision, format death, and provenance loss. Crucially, ex-post policy evaluation is possible only if the numbers used ex-ante survive: Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) could score its 7th nursing workforce projection against realized outcomes (deviations of 2.98% and 2.36% for demand and supply) only because the original projection documents remained retrievable. We present a lightweight verification-chain protocol — capture, SHA-256 hashing, independent witnessing via the Internet Archive, semantic extraction with cell-level provenance, bitemporal cataloguing, DOI deposit, and revision monitoring — and demonstrate it end-to-end on the document set of the 4th meeting of MHLW’s 2040 nursing workforce committee, in which prefecture-supplied municipal microdata were re-tabulated into secondary-medical-area statistics that exist nowhere else. All nine artifacts were captured, hashed, and independently witnessed (8/8 PDFs byte-identical to Internet Archive copies), and the embedded tables extracted under two-tier quality control (row-sum checks passed 60/60; double-entry cross-verification matched 916/916 cells), yielding a DOI-bearing dataset within one operator-day on commodity hardware. We position preservation as the precondition of accountability, and fugitive statistics as a measurable site of institutional debt: the divergence between the statistics a policy decision consumed and the statistics later available to evaluate it.

articles.title: Two Ways of Being Misled: Composition Bias, Weak Within-Municipality Progress, and a Fixed Size Gradient in Japan's Individual Evacuation Plan Statistics, 2022–2026

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Japan requires every municipality to maintain a registry of residents who cannot evacuate unaided (2013 amendment to the Disaster Countermeasures Basic Act) and, since 2021, to make best efforts to prepare an individual evacuation plan for each person listed. Progress is monitored through annual national surveys published as municipality-level tables in PDF format. We reconstruct these tables into a machine-readable panel of 1,741 municipalities across five survey waves (2022–2026; 10 source documents, plan and registry series), with documented recovery of 74 rows lost to table-rendering defects, external reconciliation of ambiguous column semantics against published national aggregates, and a complete provenance registry of corrections and known gaps. Three findings follow, and they cut in different directions. First, the pooled statistics are misleading about direction: the median creation rate across all responding municipalities falls from 19.0% to 17.8%, whereas every continuously observed subset improves, because late-entering municipalities start low and are added faster than incumbents advance. Second, and against our own initial reading, composition control does not reveal robust progress. Within the 423 municipalities observed in all five waves, the median change is only +0.77 points over four years, with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval reaching down to zero (+0.00 to +1.80; mean +3.79, CI +0.81 to +6.82; Wilcoxon p = 0.0006), and only 54.6% improved at all. The +8.3-point rise in the panel median is a shift in the position of the distribution driven by strong gains in its upper part, not the experience of a typical municipality. Third, plan creation is steeply graded by registry size in levels—the smallest quartile reaches a median of 43.3% against 9.9% for the largest—but not in growth: within-municipality change does not differ across size quartiles (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.47; municipality-fixed-effects interactions all p > 0.55). Small municipalities are ahead, not faster, and the gap shows no tendency to close. The published series is thus misleading twice over: it reports a decline where continuously observed municipalities do not decline, and it invites the inference that composition control would reveal healthy progress, which the panel does not support. We interpret this within an institutional-debt framework: the statistical encoding of an institution (survey composition, question definitions, item discontinuation) drifts away from the institutional reality it is meant to measure, and the divergence is itself measurable—but correcting the encoding does not, here, rescue the institution's performance. The panel, extraction code, and provenance registry are archived for reuse.

articles.title: The Geography of Green Deficits: Creating a 3-30-300 Measure for all UPRNs in Great Britain
articles.authors: Alex Singleton, Mark Alan Green, Meilin Shi
articles.abstract: The 3-30-300 rule has emerged as an influential benchmark for equitable urban green space provision, specifying that every home should have visibility of 3 trees, 30% neighbourhood tree canopy cover, and access to public green space within 300 metres. Despite growing international application, there is no GB-wide assessment of how households meet the rule. This paper presents the first nationally consistent operationalisation of the framework at the highest possible spatial resolution, calculating indicators for approximately 40 million Unique Property Reference Numbers (UPRNs) using high-resolution tree mapping, open green space data, and network-based pedestrian routing. We generate the 3-30-300 indicators as contin- uous measures, enabling assessment under canonical and alternative threshold specifications. Results reveal a substantial national green deficit: only 0.7% of urban UPRNs satisfy all three thresholds, with the 30% canopy criterion the binding constraint. The three components decouple both spatially and socio-economically. Tree visibility and canopy cover concen- trate in affluent southern suburbs and exhibit steep positive deprivation gradients, whereas proximity to formal green space marginally favours the most deprived urban neighbourhoods, reflecting inherited civic park provision in dense industrial- era cities. Composite compliance is nine times higher in the least deprived decile than the most deprived, a pattern robust to threshold relaxation. We argue the framework is best understood as three distinct policy levers rather than a single standard, and that place-sensitive, component-specific targeting is required to avoid widening the inequalities the rule seeks to ad- dress.

articles.title: Advancing open research information: exploring the persistence of proprietary bibliographic databases
articles.authors: Tanya Lee, Kathleen Gregory, Alexander Rushforth
articles.abstract: Purpose – “Research information”, which informs how research is searched, conducted, monitored, and evaluated, is usually made available in proprietary databases in ways which often restrict its use. Recently, there has been a movement towards opening research information through the creation of systems such as OpenAlex, but their adoption remains inconsistent. In this study, we explore challenges which university stakeholders face in switching from proprietary to open databases for research information. Design/methodology/approach – We conducted 19 semi-structured interviews with university stakeholders in the Netherlands, a particularly proactive environment in the Open Research Information movement. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and informed by literature in platform capitalism and infrastructure studies. Findings – The analysis shows that even in seemingly progressive environments, systemic change remains challenging. Longstanding routines, technical dependencies, and embedded practices present challenges for universities to disengage from proprietary databases and their complementary services. Concerns about the viability and further development of open databases became apparent through the context of collective action dilemmas perceived by interviewees. Importantly, we find that platform capitalism, a framework often employed in analyzing proprietary companies, is not sufficient to explain these hesitancies. Originality/Value – Our findings highlight the challenges faced in an under-researched area of open science: the adoption of open research information. Our study is relevant to open science advocates and for institutions struggling with similar challenges. Our analysis makes a conceptual contribution through treating claims about the platform dominance of proprietary databases as empirical questions and highlighting the importance of stakeholder agency, contingency and variation.

articles.title: Beyond Whitechapel: A Transnational Forensic Reassessment of the Jack the Ripper Murders
articles.abstract: This study presents the transnational Whitechapel linkage hypothesis, an integrated retrospective hypothesis examining whether evidence traditionally treated as unrelated may be better understood within a mobile, cross-jurisdictional offender framework. The analysis brings together the canonical Whitechapel murders of 1888, reported Rotterdam dockside killings and contemporary “Whitechapel-like” comparisons, the 1890 Mary Eleanor Wheeler Pearcey case, the testimony and subsequent archival disappearance of John Charles Pearcey, Mary Pearcey’s unusual final communications preserved in Spanish-language Fabra/Havas dispatches, the later confession attributed to a sailor using the name John Anderson, the South American voyage of the Annie Speer, and the incompletely identified 1895 Iquique death registration of Evaristo Vergara. Rather than treating any single item as dispositive, the theory uses modern forensic-psychological reasoning, behavioral case-linkage principles, temporal and geographic reconstruction, victimology, maritime mobility analysis, forensic linguistics, identity reconstruction, and alternative-hypothesis testing to ask whether the combined pattern is consistent with a mobile offender or offender network operating across port environments. The evidence presently supports a historically plausible and investigatively testable linkage model, but it does not establish a definitive identity for the Whitechapel offender. The contribution of the theory is therefore not a declaration that the case has been solved; it is a structured model explaining why the Rotterdam-London maritime corridor, the Pearcey evidence, the Anderson confession, and the Iquique records warrant examination together rather than in isolation.

articles.title: Why Workers Use AI Less Often: Reasons for Declining Workplace AI Use in Germany
articles.abstract: This short report summarizes recent findings on the extent and the change in the professional use of artificial intelligence (AI) among workers in Germany. It is based on a quota-based online survey of 2,585 workers, conducted from 29 April 2026 to 11 May 2026. The focus is on how professional AI use has changed over the past three months, what reasons are cited for reduced use, and how an increase or decrease is related to individual and organizational characteristics. The majority report that their use has remained unchanged. Overall, increases predominate, while a decrease affects only a small proportion of the workforce. A decline in usage is associated with a more critical attitude toward AI, lower perceived competence and organizational support, as well as a perceived lack of added value, unreliable results, and data privacy concerns. At the same time, social differences are evident: higher-skilled workers are more likely to increase their usage, while lower-skilled workers are comparatively more likely to reduce it. This raises the question of whether AI reduces or exacerbates existing inequalities in the workplace.

articles.title: Unionization in Higher Education: An Industry-Level View
articles.abstract: This research note presents estimates of union membership and collective bargaining coverage in the higher education industry using data from the Current Population Survey. The paper analyzes the extent of union membership and collective bargaining coverage from 1983-2025, both in the industry and among faculty specifically, and estimates of the variation in union membership by employment sector, race and gender for 2024. Using a 10-year span of data, the paper also estimates union wage premiums in the industry and among faculty. This note finds union membership and bargaining coverage has remained stable over the past four decades, but documents notable gendered and ethnoracial disparities in both measures in 2024. Faculty and industry collective bargaining results in earnings premiums ranging between 4% and 5%. The findings present quantitative estimates of unionism and its material effects for higher education workers that complement recent research published by the National Center for the Study of Collective Bargaining in Higher Education and the Professions.

articles.title: Technology–Based Rehabilitation Interventions for Children with Cerebral Palsy in Low- and Lower-Middle-Income Countries (LMICs): A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Zahra Lalani, Salena Aggerwal, Jennifer O'Neil
articles.abstract: Background: Cerebral palsy (CP) affects approximately 1.6 per 1,000 children globally. In Low- and Lower-Middle-Income Countries (LMICs), children with CP face significant barriers to rehabilitation. Emerging technology-based interventions such as 3D printing, virtual reality (VR), and telerehabilitation offer innovative, cost-effective solutions for resource-constrained settings. Objective: This scoping review explored technology-based motor rehabilitation interventions for children with CP in LMICs, identifying implementation locations, challenges, and opportunities. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus (2015–2026) identified studies on technology-based motor rehabilitation for children with CP in World Bank–defined LMICs. Following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework, two independent reviewers screened studies and extracted data on intervention types, outcomes, and LMIC implementation factors, resolving discrepancies by consensus. Results: From 2,046 screened titles, 18 studies were included across Egypt, Jordan, Pakistan, India, and Bangladesh. Interventions featured Kinect® therapy, augmented reality, Wii® exergaming, robotic-assisted gait training, biosensor-driven mechatronic devices with 3D-printed parts, and community-led telerehabilitation. Key challenges included high equipment costs, rural poverty, hardware instability, and caregiver technological unfamiliarity or overstimulation concerns. Opportunities included heightened patient motivation, objective progress monitoring to reduce reporting bias, and reduced physical burden on staff. The SMART-CP model demonstrated that integrated telerehabilitation increases service uptake, overcoming geographical and financial barriers. Conclusions: Technology-based interventions, specifically VR, augmented reality, exergames, and telerehabilitation, show strong promise for improving motor function and engagement in children with CP in LMICs. Despite cost and accessibility hurdles, these tools represent viable, scalable solutions for expanding rehabilitation services in low-resource environments.

articles.title: The cultural politics of risk: egalitarian civil society opposition to solar radiation modification
articles.authors: Julia Silvia Guivant, María Inés Carabajal, Eduardo J. Viola, Timothy Robert Silberg
articles.abstract: Solar radiation modification (SRM) has become a focus of climate research and governance debate. While much of the governance literature addresses scientific assessment, responsible research, participation, and multilateral oversight, less attention has been paid to how civil society actors shape what counts as legitimate governance. This article examines how the ETC Group and allied actors construct opposition to SRM. Drawing on Cultural Theory of Risk, sociotechnical imaginaries, and interpretive discourse analysis of public materials from 2008 to 2025, it reconstructs a predominantly egalitarian repertoire organized around the vulnerability of nature and affected communities, distrust of concentrated expertise and corporate power, and claims concerning consent, sovereignty, and environmental justice. Hierarchical, individualist, and fatalist registers are incorporated into this repertoire in distinct ways: authority is aﬀirmed when it supports limits, private initiative marks the adversary, and lock-in supplies the warning scenario. Three practices give this politics of refusal coherence: translating soft law into non-use, contesting field experiments as steps toward normalization, and constructing counter-expertise. The analysis shows that this position has political force because it exposes risks of normalization and concentrated authority. It also has crucial governance limits, narrowing the space in which research, assessment, participation, and Southern agency can be distinguished and debated.

articles.title: Learning the Language of Academia
articles.authors: August Lohse, Frederik Laursen Nielsen, Snorre Ralund, Felix Weiss
articles.abstract: Much of students’ performance in higher education is evaluated through written assignments and examinations. Mastering academic language is therefore not only an important part of learning at university but also central to how students are assessed. This article examines how two important features of academic writing, textual complexity and idea density, are related to university grades and how students develop these over time. Using nine years of longitudinal exam data from Danish universities, we apply natural language processing techniques to measure these textual features in close to 250,000 student submissions. The findings show that writing complexity and idea density are both highly related to grades, and that students write increasingly complex and idea-dense submissions over time at university. We further examine whether learning trajectories differ across ethnolinguistic groups and whether such differences help explain ethnic disparities in academic performance. Students with non-Danish ethnolinguistic backgrounds generally begin their studies with lower levels of textual complexity and idea density, but they improve more rapidly than students with Danish backgrounds. Despite this convergence, students with non-Danish backgrounds receive lower grades on average, and accounting for the measured textual features explains only a small part of the grade gap.
